verdict.summary: The seccomp filter fails open when rules are not installed: seccomp_rule_add errors other than exactly -EFAULT are silently ignored in both blocklist loops, and all seccomp_rule_add_exact results for the socket-family allowlist are ignored. limitations: Only the provided snippet was analyzed; helper behavior (CudaSolver::GetScratchSpace, flat_inner_dims exact semantics, Tensor::dim_size DCHECK placement) was reasoned from standard TensorFlow patterns.

verdict.summary: The XML node parser dereferences the scanner cursor (and cursor+1) without EOF/bounds checks in several paths, causing out-of-bounds reads on empty or truncated input; it applies an unconditional 'slen -= 2' to attribute values, which underflows lengths for unquoted values; and it recurses without a depth limit for nested elements and PI/comment constructs, enabling stack-exhaustion denial of service.

evidence.snippet:
if (*scanner->curptr != '<')
	on_syntax_error(scanner);
evidence.reason: Dereferences *scanner->curptr with no pj_scan_is_eof() guard; on empty/truncated input curptr == end, reading one byte past the buffer (CWE-125).

evidence.snippet: if (*scanner->curptr=='?' && *(scanner->curptr+1)=='>') { ... } return xml_parse_node(pool, scanner);
evidence.reason: PI handling reads curptr+1 without bounds checks after a scan-until loop that may stop at EOF, and recurses once per PI construct; many PIs cause unbounded recursion and stack exhaustion (CWE-125, CWE-674).

evidence.snippet: while (*scanner->curptr != '>' && *scanner->curptr != '/') { ... }
evidence.reason: Attribute loop condition dereferences the cursor with no EOF check after name scanning can consume to EOF, yielding an out-of-bounds read; no bound on attribute count enables memory-exhaustion.
Unconditionally strips two quote characters; for unquoted values (e.g. <a x=y>) the token has no quotes, so slen underflows to a negative/wrong length and corrupts string-length metadata (CWE-191).

evidence.snippet: while (*scanner->curptr == '<' && *(scanner->curptr+1) != '/' && *(scanner->curptr+1) != '!') { pj_xml_node *sub_node = xml_parse_node(pool, scanner); ... }
evidence.reason: Condition dereferences curptr+1 without bounds checks (OOB read if input ends in '<'), and recursion depth is unbounded, so deeply nested XML exhausts the stack (CWE-125, CWE-674).

evidence.snippet: while (pj_scan_strcmp(scanner, "]]>", 3)) { ... }
evidence.reason: CDATA loop reads 3 bytes at the cursor with no EOF check; unterminated <![CDATA[ input causes an out-of-bounds read and unsafe length recomputation (CWE-125).

assumptions: The pj_scan_get_until_ch / pj_scan_get_until_chr helpers can stop at EOF without raising, leaving curptr == end for subsequent direct dereferences.
The input buffer is not guaranteed to have a NUL or slack byte after scanner->end, so reads at curptr/curptr+1 are genuinely out of bounds.
on_syntax_error may unwind via the parsing exception mechanism, but the unchecked dereferences occur before it can fire or on paths where it is not called.
limitations: Exact implementations of pj_scan_get_char, pj_scan_get_quotes, pj_scan_get_until_ch, and pj_scan_strcmp are not provided, so precise reachability and extent of the OOB reads depend on their EOF behavior.
Impact (local DoS vs. memory corruption) also depends on how callers use parsed node/attr values after this function returns.

verdict.summary: The per-slice quantization path indexes input_min_range/input_max_range and the allocated min/max output tensors by i up to num_slices-1 without validating that those tensors contain num_slices elements. Attacker-controlled tensor shapes can therefore cause out-of-bounds reads (min_ranges(i)/max_ranges(i)) and out-of-bounds writes (output_min_tensor->flat<float>()(i)) on the heap. axis_ is also not validated against the input rank.

evidence.reason: Loop index i is bounded only by num_slices, never by the element counts of the min/max range tensors or of the allocated min/max output tensors; if any of these have fewer than num_slices elements, the accesses are out of bounds (OOB read CWE-125, OOB write CWE-787).

There is no OP_REQUIRES validating that input(1)/input(2) contain exactly num_slices elements and that minmax_shape is {num_slices}; the unchecked mismatch between minmax_shape and num_slices enables the out-of-bounds writes in the quantization loop.

axis_ is not checked to be within [0, input.dims()); an out-of-range axis feeds dim_size(axis_) and later flat_inner_outer_dims(axis_ - 1), leading to undefined shape handling and inconsistent num_slices.

assumptions: axis_ and mode_ are pre-parsed member variables set from op attributes before Compute runs.
The code excerpt omits any earlier OP_REQUIRES that would validate min/max range shapes; the analysis is based solely on the shown code.
QuantizeSlice/QuantizeTensor are assumed to write exactly the elements of the chip/pointer passed to them.
limitations: No file path or original line numbers were provided; line numbers are approximate positions in the excerpt.

The behavior of input.dim_size() and bit_casted_shaped() for invalid ranks depends on the enclosing TensorFlow version and build (DCHECK vs release), so the axis_ issue risks undefined behavior rather than a single deterministic fault.
The int64 overflow of pre_dim/post_dim products is noted as a secondary risk but is not the primary finding.

verdict.summary: No memory-safety vulnerability is present in the given function: every destination write uses strlcpy/snprintf with a size bounded to the actual destination array, guarantees NUL termination, and cap->reserved is explicitly zeroed. The only residual risk, an out-of-bounds read if dev->card_label is not NUL-terminated, depends on initialization code outside this function.

evidence.snippet: int labellen = (sizeof(cap->card) < sizeof(dev->card_label)) ? sizeof(cap->card) : sizeof(dev->card_label);
evidence.reason: Size bound is the minimum of source and destination array sizes and is always positive, so it cannot exceed the 32-byte cap->card buffer.

evidence.snippet: snprintf(cap->card, labellen, "%s", dev->card_label);
evidence.reason: Bounded write into cap->card with NUL termination guaranteed; no overflow. Read of card_label via %s assumes NUL termination, which is established by code not shown here.

evidence.snippet: snprintf(cap->bus_info, sizeof(cap->bus_info), "platform:v4l2loopback-%03d", device_nr);
evidence.reason: Write limited to sizeof(cap->bus_info); extreme device_nr values only cause truncation, never an overflow.

evidence.snippet: memset(cap->reserved, 0, sizeof(cap->reserved));
evidence.reason: Reserved bytes are zeroed, closing the common kernel-info-leak path through uninitialized capability padding.

assumptions: dev->vdev and its video_get_drvdata pointer are non-NULL when this ioctl handler runs.
dev->card_label is NUL-terminated by its initializer/setter (not visible in this snippet).
On kernels >= 3.1, the v4l2 core sets cap->version after the handler returns, and the ioctl layer manages buffer zeroing before the copy to user space.
limitations: Initialization of dev->card_label is not shown, so the OOB-read condition of the %s format cannot be fully verified from this code alone.
The preprocessor branches (kernel version checks) mean the exact set of initialized fields varies by kernel; the analysis assumes the v4l2 core fills version/device_caps as commented.
Potential NULL-pointer dereference of dev->vdev/drvdata would be a robustness issue but is not user-controlled and is not exposed by the shown logic.

verdict.summary: AssignOp performs the final data copy on a buffer re-read after releasing the input-ref mutex, without re-validating that its size still matches rhs. When validate_shape_ is false and the variable is concurrently resized/reassigned, rhs data can be copied into an undersized buffer (out-of-bounds heap write), and even without a resize the unlocked write races with concurrent readers/writers. A failed Tensor::CopyFrom also aborts the process via CHECK.

evidence.snippet:
Tensor old_unlocked_lhs = context->mutable_input(0, /* lock_held */ false);
Copy(context, &old_unlocked_lhs, rhs);
evidence.reason: TOCTOU: the element-count/shape check was performed under the mutex (lines 24, 40-41), but this copy re-reads the variable without the lock and without re-checking size. A concurrent reassignment with a smaller buffer (allowed when validate_shape_ is false) makes Copy write rhs-sized data out of bounds.

When use_exclusive_lock_ is false this branch falls through to the unlocked copy at lines 82-83, leaving the variable exposed to a concurrent resize/read while the copy is in flight (data race, potential OOB write).

evidence.snippet: CHECK(reshaped_old_lhs.CopyFrom(old_lhs, rhs.shape()));
evidence.reason: CHECK aborts the whole process if CopyFrom fails; it is guarded by a prior num_elements equality check in the current control flow, but any future divergence (or a shape/element-count edge case) turns an input-driven condition into a denial-of-service crash.

assumptions: Exploitation requires concurrent mutation of the ref variable and validate_shape_ == false (or a concurrent read/consumer while the unlocked copy runs).
Tensor buffers are refcounted shallow copies, so use-after-free via this path is not expected; the primary memory-safety risk is out-of-bounds writes from a size mismatch at copy time.
LHS/RHS dtype mismatch is not validated in this function but is effectively constrained by per-dtype kernel registration.
limitations: The exact concurrency contract of use_exclusive_lock_ is defined outside this function; upstream TensorFlow documents unlocked assignment behavior as undefined when the caller does not guarantee exclusivity.
No explicit line numbers were provided; line numbers are approximate based on the snippet layout.
Analysis is based only on the supplied code, not on surrounding kernel registration, thread-safety guarantees, or Tensor/Copy implementation details.

verdict.summary: Module path is built from unvalidated `info->name` (and `dir`), canonicalized by `realpath`, and opened read-only, allowing path traversal/arbitrary file read if the module name is attacker-controlled. A separate out-of-bounds read occurs when `dir->length == 0` and `info->name.length > 0` because the `length == 0` guard returns only when both lengths are zero, yet `dir->start[dir->length - 1]` is still evaluated. The `realpath`/`open` pair is also subject to TOCTOU, and `open` lacks `O_CLOEXEC`.

evidence.reason: The guard returns only when `dir->length + name.length == 0`. If `dir->length == 0` and `name.length > 0`, the code reads `dir->start[SIZE_MAX]` (underflowed index), an out-of-bounds read whose value controls `trail` and the path separator.

`info->name` is embedded into the path with no validation of `..`, absolute paths, or null bytes in the length window, and `realpath` then canonicalizes it before `open` — enabling traversal outside the module directory and arbitrary read of any accessible file.

The canonicalized path string is resolved and then opened in separate operations, creating a TOCTOU window where an attacker can replace the file after `realpath` validation. Also, `realpath` writes up to `PATH_MAX` bytes into `info->path` whose size is not bounded in this code.

evidence.snippet: info->fd = open(&info->path[0], O_RDONLY);
evidence.reason: `open` is called without `O_CLOEXEC`, so the descriptor can leak into child processes (fd leak), and there is no fd reuse protection for subsequent exec.
`length` is a `size_t` and only compared against `NJS_MAX_PATH` after unchecked additions; an overflow could bypass the size check. Low likelihood given realistic length values.

assumptions: `info->name` and `dir` may be attacker-influenced (e.g., derived from untrusted module specifiers); caller-side validation is not visible in this snippet.
`info->path` is a fixed buffer whose exact size is not shown; if it is not at least `PATH_MAX` bytes, `realpath` can overflow it.
limitations: Caller context (who supplies `dir` and `info->name`) is out of scope, so exploitability of the path traversal depends on trust boundaries.
Whether `dir->length == 0` can occur in practice depends on callers; the OOB read is definite only for that input condition.
`njs_cpymem` and `NJS_MAX_PATH` semantics are assumed to be memcpy-like and PATH_MAX-sized, respectively.

verdict.summary: The session-ID digest is built by concatenating variable-length validation settings (CA digest, verify_certificate_hash_list_, verify_certificate_spki_list_) with no length prefixes or separators. Distinct configurations can therefore produce identical byte streams and identical digests. Because session resumption is keyed on this digest, a session created under looser validation settings may be resumed after stricter settings are active, bypassing certificate validation (CWE-345).

evidence.reason: Variable-length certificate and SPKI hashes are streamed into the digest as a bare concatenation without length framing, counts, or type tags. Different list contents/orders can yield identical byte streams and identical session-ID digests, so sessions can be resumed across configurations with different validation strictness.

The CA-certificate digest is appended with no length or separator, creating ambiguity at the boundary between the CA digest and the subsequent hash-list bytes. An attacker-controlled or coincidental byte sequence can make two different configurations hash identically.

SAN matchers are reduced to a pre-hashed size_t before inclusion, shrinking the effective entropy and adding an additional collision surface on top of the missing length framing; a secondary contributor to digest collisions between distinct configurations.

assumptions: verify_certificate_hash_list_ and verify_certificate_spki_list_ contain variable-length elements as the surrounding code and the sizeof-based length computation imply.
The resulting digest is used to bind TLS session resumption to the current certificate-validation configuration (per the function comment).
limitations: Code outside this function (session-cache lookup, ticket lifetimes, re-validation on resume) is not shown, so the exact exploitability depends on the surrounding session-management logic.
hash.size() * sizeof(value_type) overflow is theoretically possible only with impractically large vectors or wide value types; not treated as a primary finding.
Whether any real-world configuration pair collides in practice requires enumerating the actual setting combinations; the flaw is in the framing, not in a demonstrated collision.

verdict.summary: The VM dispatches bytecode operands as unchecked indices and counts into irep->pool, irep->syms, irep->reps, and the register stack, and OP_JMPUW computes an absolute jump target that is not validated against irep->ilen on the main dispatch path. Malformed or untrusted bytecode can trigger out-of-bounds reads/writes (register stack, pool, symbol table, child-irep table) and redirect execution outside the instruction stream, enabling memory corruption and potentially arbitrary code execution.

evidence.snippet: const mrb_irep *nirep = irep->reps[b];
evidence.reason: OP_LAMBDA/OP_BLOCK/OP_METHOD index irep->reps with the 16-bit operand b and no check against irep->rlen. A crafted operand yields an out-of-range child irep pointer; the subsequent dereferences of nirep->iseq/nregs/pool/syms drive wild memory access and control-flow setup.

evidence.snippet: a = (uint32_t)((pc - irep->iseq) + (int16_t)a); ... pc = irep->iseq + a; JUMP;
evidence.reason: OP_JMPUW main path jumps to irep->iseq + a without verifying the target lies in [0, irep->ilen). The bounds assertion exists only in the CHECKPOINT_RESTORE path, so a malicious offset (or missing ensure handler) lets execution escape the instruction stream.

evidence.snippet: regs[a] = mrb_ary_new_from_values(mrb, b, &regs[a]);
evidence.reason: OP_ARRAY copies b registers from regs[a] with no check that a+b is within the current frame size. OP_HASH (lim = a+b*2) and OP_ARYPUSH (loop over b values from regs[a+i+1]) have the same unchecked count->size conversion, causing out-of-bounds stack reads/writes.

evidence.snippet: SET_SYM_VALUE(regs[a], syms[b]);
evidence.reason: OP_LOADSYM and the GV/SV/IV/CV accessors dereference irep->syms[b] without validating b against irep->slen, allowing out-of-bounds symbol-table reads that propagate bogus symbol IDs into property/global access routines.

evidence.snippet: if (e && b < MRB_ENV_LEN(e)) { *regs_a = e->stack[b]; }
evidence.reason: OP_GETUPVAR/OP_SETUPVAR demonstrate the bounds-check discipline literally present elsewhere in the same function; the unchecked pool/syms/reps/regs indexing shown above violates that invariant and is the actual defect.

assumptions: The executing irep (iseq, pool, syms, reps, nlocals/nregs) is supplied by an untrusted or malformed source; loader-side validation is not part of this snippet and is not re-verified here.
Run-time operands a, b, c and derived counts are treated as trusted by the dispatch loop.
Line numbers are unavailable for this fragment, so location fields are null.
limitations: Several macros (FETCH_*, ARGUMENT_NORMALIZE, cipush, mrb_stack_extend, mrb_ary_new_from_values) are not shown, limiting full verification of stack resizing and argument normalization.
If all ireps are guaranteed to be compiler-generated and loader-validated, the listed indices stay in bounds; the vulnerabilities require malformed/untrusted bytecode.
Exploitability depends on allocator layout, GC behavior, and whether mrb_assert is compiled in on the CHECKPOINT_RESTORE path.

verdict.summary: Argument validation is ordered incorrectly: the early-return guard `if (len == 0 || n == 0)` runs before the `n < 0` check, so calling shift with a negative count on an empty array returns an empty array instead of raising ArgumentError. The flaw is confined to input validation; n is never used in memory operations on this path, so no out-of-bounds access or memory corruption is reachable.

evidence.snippet:
if (len == 0 || n == 0) return mrb_ary_new(mrb);
if (n < 0) mrb_raise(mrb, E_ARGUMENT_ERROR, "negative array shift");
evidence.reason: With len == 0 and n < 0, the first guard short-circuits the return, bypassing the negative-count validation. The negative check should precede the empty/short-circuit check so invalid input is rejected consistently regardless of array length.

assumptions: mrb_get_args with format "|i" writes n only when an argument is present and returns 0 otherwise; non-integer arguments raise before n is used.
ARY_LEN/ARY_PTR return the logical length and a valid in-bounds pointer (embedded buffer or heap allocation) sized for the current length.
ARY_SHIFT_SHARED_MIN is larger than the embedded-array capacity, so embedded arrays take the in-place shift branch, and ary_make_shared always yields a valid heap pointer for the L_SHIFT path.

limitations: Static analysis only; code was not compiled or executed.
The snippet is isolated; surrounding definitions, GC/arena interactions outside this function, and upstream comparison were not verifiable in the provided context.
The identified flaw is behavioral/validation-only; no memory-safety impact was identified on any reachable path.

verdict.summary: Matrix dimensions from int64 dim_size() are narrowed to int without range checks. Truncated values can make the k == k2 compatibility check pass for genuinely unequal inner dimensions and can allocate an undersized output, allowing Eigen's contract to read out of bounds from the right operand and write out of bounds of the output tensor.

evidence.reason: dim_size() returns int64; assigning to int truncates large dimensions silently. No INT_MAX bounds check is performed before the values are used for the k == k2 invariant and output allocation.

evidence.snippet: OP_REQUIRES(ctx, k == k2, errors::InvalidArgument("Matrix size incompatible: a: ", a.shape().DebugString(), ", b: ", b.shape().DebugString()));
evidence.reason: The compatibility gate compares already-truncated int values, so unequal real dimensions that narrow to the same int (e.g., 2^32+5 and 5) pass the check, letting Eigen contract operate on mismatched matrices.

evidence.snippet: OP_REQUIRES_OK(ctx, ctx->allocate_output(0, TensorShape({m, n}), &output));
evidence.reason: Output buffer is sized from truncated m/n. If a real dimension exceeds INT_MAX, the allocated buffer is smaller than the actual matrix, so the subsequent contract writes out of bounds.

assumptions: dim_size() returns int64, matching TensorFlow's Tensor API used by OpKernelContext-based kernels.
An attacker can control tensor shapes supplied to this kernel.
limitations: Exact exploitability depends on Eigen's runtime dimension validation in the contract evaluation path, which is not shown here.
Line numbers were not provided in the code excerpt, so locations are null.

verdict.summary: In the SVC slice branch the return value of svc_parse_slice() is discarded; when parsing fails (e.g., slice references a missing SPS, or sps_id is out of range) n_state.sps can be NULL, and the unconditional avc_compute_poc(&n_state) dereferences it, yielding a NULL pointer dereference and a denial of service from craftable NAL input. Additionally, the regular slice path dereferences n_state.sps while only validating the previous state's avc->s_info.sps pointer.

evidence.reason: Unchecked (discarded) return from svc_parse_slice: on failure due to missing/unknown SPS, n_state.sps may be NULL, then avc_compute_poc() dereferences n_state.sps->poc_type unconditionally -> NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476), reachable via a crafted SVC slice NAL before any SPS is stored in avc->sps[].

Only the previous state's SPS pointer (avc->s_info.sps) is NULL-checked; the newly parsed n_state.sps is dereferenced without its own check after avc_parse_slice() may have replaced the pointer. Safe in current GPAC only because avc_parse_slice() returns -1 when the SPS is missing; any future/alternate helper that succeeds with n_state.sps == NULL would dereference NULL here.

evidence.reason: No EOF/error check on the NAL header read; a failed read yields 0 and is treated as a valid NAL type, so parsing continues on truncated input (correctness/robustness issue, not directly memory-unsafe).

assumptions: avc_compute_poc() dereferences si->sps->poc_type unconditionally, as in GPAC media_tools/av_parsers.c.
svc_parse_slice() returns a negative error and/or leaves si->sps NULL when sps_id > 31 or avc->sps[sps_id] == NULL.

verdict.summary: Chunk offset bounds checks add sizeof(int)*5 (tiled) or sizeof(int)*2 (scanline) to attacker-controlled tinyexr_uint64 offsets without overflow checking. Near-UINT64_MAX offsets wrap the sum, bypass the '> size' guard, underflow data_size, and lead to out-of-bounds pointer arithmetic (head + offset) and out-of-bounds reads of line_no/data_len, after which wrapped data_len is passed to the pixel decoders. Additional signed-overflow UB exists in scanline block math and the total-size overflow guard is omitted on 32-bit builds.

Same wrap-around flaw in the tiled path: a near-UINT64_MAX block offset wraps offsets[tile_idx] + 20, bypasses the guard, underflows data_size, and lets file-controlled data_len pass validation while DecodeTiledPixelData reads from out-of-bounds memory.

const bool total_data_len_overflown = sizeof(void*) == 8 ? (total_data_len >= 0x4000000000) : false;

verdict.summary: The digest length returned by digest_length(d) is stored in a signed int and used without validation as the size for xmalloc and crypto_memneq. A negative or erroneous length becomes a huge size_t, causing a massive allocation/abort or an out-of-bounds read of md and tmp; a zero length makes the comparison trivially succeed and return 0, falsely reporting verification success. Additionally, the computed digest buffer is freed without zeroization, leaving potentially sensitive keyed-digest material in heap memory.

evidence.reason: Signed return value is used as a size with no check that it is positive; a negative/zero value flows into allocation and comparison lengths.

evidence.snippet: tmp = xmalloc(len);
evidence.reason: Negative len converts to a huge size_t allocation request, enabling denial of service or an inconsistent buffer if allocation succeeds.

The comparison length is attacker-influenced via len without bounds validation: a huge length causes out-of-bounds reads of md and tmp; a zero length compares equal and returns success without verifying the digest.
The digest buffer is freed without explicit zeroization, leaving sensitive computed digest material in heap memory for potential recovery.

assumptions: digest_length(d) may return a non-positive value (e.g., an error) for some states of d, since no contract is shown.
xmalloc aborts on allocation failure rather than returning NULL.
crypto_memneq is assumed to be the constant-time comparison; if it were memcmp, a timing side-channel would also apply.
digest_final returns 0 on success and fills len bytes, and the caller guarantees md points to at least len bytes.
limitations: Only the given code is analyzed; the behavior of digest_length, digest_final, xmalloc, and crypto_memneq is inferred from naming conventions.
Whether the negative-length path is reachable depends on how digest contexts are constructed and validated by callers.

verdict.summary: ECDSA signing performs the scalar multiplication EccPoint_mult with the raw nonce k before any randomization, and the randomized blinding is applied only to the subsequent modular inversion (and degrades to identity when no RNG is configured). evidence.reason: The nonce k (adjusted only by adding n/2n, a public constant) is used directly in the scalar multiplication, the most timing-sensitive operation. The random blinding performed later only protects uECC_vli_modInv, so timing leakage of EccPoint_mult exposes nonce bits, enabling private-key recovery via biased/reused-nonce ECDSA attacks (CWE-208/CWE-203).

When no RNG is configured, tmp=1 makes the side-channel countermeasure an identity operation; the modular inversion then runs directly on the raw nonce k with data-dependent timing/branching, silently disabling the intended protection.

verdict.summary: mrb_vm_exec trusts bytecode operands without bounds validation: OP_SETIDX unconditionally writes regs[a+3] (heap OOB write), OP_LOADL/OP_LOADSYM/OP_LAMBDA and relatives index pool/syms/reps tables unchecked (OOB read), relative jumps can move pc outside iseq, OP_ARGARY and OP_BLKPUSH have an off-by-one env-length guard when reading keyword slots, and OP_SEND uses the uninitialized local 'blk' as a proc. Executing untrusted or malformed irep can corrupt memory, read out of bounds, or cause type confusion/crash; compiler-generated bytecode normally respects the assumed invariants.

evidence.reason: Unconditional write at regs[a+3] with no check that the stack frame covers index a+3; large/malformed 'a' yields a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).
'blk' is never initialized before being read as an mrb_value and treated as a proc; an uninitialized/garbage tag can pass mrb_proc_p() and lead to dereferencing an invalid pointer (CWE-457).
Guard only ensures LEN >= m1+r+m2+2, but the kd read of stack[m1+r+m2+1] equals e->stack[m1+r+m2+2], one slot past the env when LEN == m1+r+m2+2 (CWE-125 off-by-one).
Same off-by-one guard: with kd set and LEN == m1+r+m2+2, stack[m1+r+m2+1] reads e->stack[m1+r+m2+2] out of bounds (CWE-125).

Relative/absolute jump targets are not validated against irep->ilen except inside mrb_assert (removed in NDEBUG builds); a crafted offset moves pc outside iseq, making the next fetch an OOB access (CWE-125/CWE-787).
pool, syms, and reps are indexed by opcode operand without runtime bounds checks; malformed irep causes out-of-bounds heap reads (CWE-125).
OP_ENTER reads regs[mrb_ci_bidx(ci)] and copies 15 values from &regs[1] without confirming the frame size, an OOB read for undersized frames (CWE-125).

assumptions: Bytecode (irep) may be loaded from an untrusted source, e.g., via mrb_load_irep of a crafted/malicious binary.
Builds use NDEBUG so mrb_assert checks are compiled out.
Helper macros not shown (FETCH_*, ARGUMENT_NORMALIZE, uvenv, cipush/cipop, mrb_stack_extend) follow the mruby 3.x definitions.
limitations: Several helper functions and macros referenced by this snippet were not provided, so exact exploitability of each path cannot be fully confirmed here.
Compiler-generated bytecode normally satisfies the assumed framing/table invariants, so these issues require malformed or untrusted bytecode.
Line numbers were omitted because they depend on the exact source revision of mrb_vm_exec.

verdict.summary: Unsound stack-slot bookkeeping in gen_assignment for NODE_CALL/NODE_SCALL (nil-safe call) and NODE_COLON2 assignment LHS. A forward OP_JMPNIL is emitted before RHS/argument pushes, stack depth is restored via s->sp = top after the send, and sp/top/call are reused as register indices after push/pop sequences without bounds checks against nregs. Crafted assignments (e.g., a&.b = c, op-assign with NULL rhs, splat/keyword args) can make codegen emit instructions reading/writing uninitialized or out-of-range VM stack slots, leading to heap buffer overflow at VM execution.

evidence.reason: For NODE_SCALL a forward conditional jump is emitted before the RHS value and arguments are pushed. When the jump is taken at runtime, those pushes never occur, but codegen later sets s->sp = top (line 161) as if they had; on the val/rhs paths the value slot top is read/written with stale or uninitialized data, and register indices derived from sp can exceed the frame size implied by nregs, producing out-of-bounds stack access.

When rhs is NULL the top slot is filled from the caller-supplied sp with gen_move(cursp(), sp, 0), and afterwards s->sp is forcibly reset to call and then to top. sp, top, and call are reused as emitted-operand indices after multiple push/pop_n sequences (including pop_n(14)/OP_ARYPUSH splat and keyword normalization) with no bounds check against s->nregs; a mismatch between modeled and actual stack depth makes the VM read/write slots outside the allocated frame (heap buffer overflow).

The constant-store OP_SETMCNST reuses sp as a stack index after push()/pop_n(2) have changed the modeled depth; sp is only relocated when it is nonzero, and with rhs NULL the assigned value exists only in the caller-provided slot. If container or RHS codegen changes the stack depth differently than modeled, the emitted operand indexes a dead or out-of-range slot, contributing to the same under-accounted nregs / heap out-of-bounds condition.

assumptions: sp is passed by callers as an index into the current codegen stack frame and is not revalidated inside gen_assignment.
irep frame size (nregs) is derived from the maximum compile-time stack depth s->sp, so instructions referencing slots above the modeled depth can exceed the allocated frame at VM execution.
Compilation inputs (ASTs) originate from untrusted Ruby source, making codegen a reachable attack surface.
limitations: Caller dispatch for NODE_ASGN/NODE_OP_ASGN and the semantics of helpers (gen_move, pop_n, genjmp2_0, dispatch, gen_values) are not included, so the exact minimal triggering AST could not be replayed in this scope.
No loop structures exist in the snippet; loop-related reasoning is not applicable.
Actual out-of-bounds reachability depends on concrete nregs accounting in the enclosing codegen_scope, which is not visible here.

verdict.summary: ex_copy trusts caller-supplied line1/line2/n without validating them against the buffer's line count, and ignores ml_append()/vim_strsave() failures. This permits signed integer overflow in count = line2 - line1 + 1 and n + count (corrupting b_op_end and appended-lines marks), and allows ml_get(line1) to read beyond the buffer's line table when line2 exceeds the buffer size or when a skipped append causes the loop's index adjustments to outrun the actual buffer contents (out-of-bounds read).

evidence.reason: No validation that line1 <= line2 or that line numbers fit in linenr_T; count and n+count can be negative or overflow, feeding corrupted values into b_op_end and subsequent undo/mark handling (CWE-190).

ml_get(line1) is called without ensuring line1 <= ml_line_count, enabling an out-of-bounds heap read when line2 exceeds the buffer or the append-index bookkeeping outruns the buffer (CWE-125). ml_append()'s FAIL return is ignored, so failed inserts are assumed successful; when vim_strsave() fails the line is skipped but the loop still advances all indices as if it were inserted.

The precomputed count is used even when appends were skipped or overflowed, so marked/undo ranges and the reported message can cover lines that were never inserted, corrupting buffer marks and change range state.

assumptions: line1, line2, and n originate from command-line input and are not pre-validated by the (unshown) caller.
linenr_T is a signed long; overflow of count and n+count is signed UB.
ml_get()/ml_append() behave as in Vim: ml_get trusts the line number, and ml_append can fail without inserting a line.
limitations: Callers or surrounding code may clamp addresses before ex_copy is invoked; the snippet itself contains no such validation.
The exact heap impact depends on ml_get()/ml_append() implementations and build flags (asserts may abort instead of reading out of bounds).
Precise source line numbers were not available in the provided snippet, so locations are omitted.

verdict.summary: QPaintEngineEx::stroke() iterates the points buffer using `points < lastPoint` as the only loop bound, while advancing the independent element-type cursor `types` (and reading up to points[0..5] per CurveToElement) without any validation of QVectorPath's internal consistency. A malformed QVectorPath (publicly constructible with arbitrary element/point arrays) can cause an infinite loop when *types is an unexpected value such as CurveToDataElement (default: break advances no cursor), an out-of-bounds read of the types array when it is shorter than the elements implied by the points buffer, or an out-of-bounds read of points in the CurveToElement case when fewer than 6 qreals remain. Implicit-close handling dereferences path.points()[0..1] and can null-dereference if points is null with elementCount()>0.

Unexpected element types (CurveToDataElement or invalid enums) take the default branch and advance neither cursor, causing an unbounded loop (CWE-835); a types array shorter than the elements implied by the points buffer is read past its end (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: The CurveToElement case unconditionally reads points[0..5] while the loop guard only guarantees at least one point-pair remains; with a malformed path whose final element type is a curve but fewer than 6 qreals remain, this reads past the end of the points buffer (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: Implicit-close handling dereferences path.points()[0..1] after only checking path.isEmpty(); a QVectorPath with elementCount()>0 but a null points pointer (legal to construct) causes a null-pointer dereference, while only count==0 is guarded (CWE-476-adjacent, subsumed under the missing-input-validation finding).

Well-formed Qt-internal paths satisfy the 2-qreal-per-element invariant, which is why normal usage does not trigger the issues.

verdict.summary: do_put computes heap allocation sizes with signed 32-bit int arithmetic (totlen + oldlen + 1, and col + yanklen + 1) that can wrap when pasting large registers or counts into long lines, producing undersized allocations that are subsequently overrun by memmove/STRMOVE/STRCPY writes, resulting in a heap buffer overflow. The existing guards bound only the multiplication products, not the full allocation-size expression.

evidence.reason: The guard bounds only totlen (int). The allocation size totlen + oldlen + 1 is computed in signed int and can wrap when oldlen is also large, yielding an undersized heap buffer. The later memmove operations write totlen + oldlen - delcount + 1 bytes, overrunning the buffer (CWE-190 -> CWE-122).

count > INT_MAX / yanklen bounds totlen = count * yanklen, but alloc(totlen + oldlen + 1) can still wrap in int. The loop plus STRMOVE write totlen + oldlen + 1 bytes in total, overflowing the wrapped (undersized) allocation.

In the multi-line MCHAR split path, alloc(col + yanklen + 1) uses int arithmetic; a very deep column combined with a large register line can wrap the size, repeating the undersized-allocation/overflow pattern. yanklen = (int)STRLEN(...) also truncates size_t, and negative results propagate into (size_t)yanklen memmove lengths.

assumptions: int and colnr_T are 32-bit and size_t is 64-bit, so signed int expressions such as totlen + oldlen + 1 and col + yanklen + 1 can wrap.
count and the register payload (y_array sizes) are treated as attacker-influenced inputs (command count, yanked text, expression result, clipboard).

limitations: No exact line numbers or build configuration were provided; symbol widths (int/colnr_T/size_t) are assumed.

verdict.summary: Integer overflow in load_image: the sanity check divides by G_MAXSIZE (64-bit gsize), but the subsequent allocations and loop bounds compute bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes in 32-bit guint32 arithmetic. Crafted .gbr/.gpb headers (e.g., 32768 x 32768 x 4 or x 2, which wrap to 0) pass validation, produce an undersized heap allocation via g_malloc, and then trigger out-of-bounds writes (case 1 pattern copy and case 2 float16 conversion) and out-of-bounds reads (gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect), enabling memory corruption and potential code execution from a malicious brush file.

evidence.snippet:
if ((bh.width == 0) || (bh.width > GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE) ||
    (bh.height == 0) || (bh.height > GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE) ||
    ((bh.bytes != 1) && (bh.bytes != 2) && (bh.bytes != 4) &&
     (bh.bytes != 18)) ||
    (G_MAXSIZE / bh.width / bh.height / bh.bytes < 1))
evidence.reason: The guard uses G_MAXSIZE (64-bit gsize) arithmetic, which on 64-bit builds only rejects products >= 2^64. Since width/height are capped far below that, products up to ~2^35 pass even though the later size calculation overflows 32-bit unsigned arithmetic.

bh.width, bh.height, and bh.bytes are guint32, so the product is computed modulo 2^32 and wraps (e.g. 32768*32768*4 = 2^32 -> 0). g_malloc(0) succeeds and read(fd, buf, 0) == 0 passes the check, leaving an undersized buffer for later loops and gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect.

4 * bh.width * bh.height is computed in 32-bit arithmetic and wraps (2^32 -> 0) for width=height=32768. The loop then performs up to ph.width*ph.height (~2^30) 3-byte reads and 1-byte writes into the undersized heap buffer, causing out-of-bounds writes and reads.

When bh.bytes == 2 and the size product wrapped (e.g. width=height=32768 -> size=0), the loop reads *buf (2 bytes per iteration) beyond the undersized allocation and writes brush_buf[i] past it, yielding out-of-bounds read and heap write.

assumptions: BrushHeader fields (header_size, version, width, height, bytes, magic_number, spacing) are guint32, consistent with the g_ntohl byte swapping.
GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE is <= 2^15 (32768) such that width*height*bytes can reach or exceed 2^32 while still passing the size guard.
Line numbers are approximate, derived from the provided snippet; the exact file name is not supplied.
gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect consumes width*height*bpp bytes from brush_buf.
limitations: The code sample is a partial function; surrounding definitions (BrushHeader layout, GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE value, platform gsize width) are not shown.
Whether exploitation leads to code execution depends on the surrounding allocator and hardening; memory corruption and heap out-of-bounds access are certain given a wrapped size.
Minor issues (ignored lseek return, missing close(fd) on some early-return paths, partial-read handling) are noted but not the focus.

verdict.summary: The Parallels image open path validates the catalog size against INT_MAX/4 before computing catalog_size*4, preventing the integer overflow that would otherwise cause an undersized g_malloc followed by an oversized bdrv_pread heap overwrite. Header reads target fixed-size stack buffers, the catalog loop is in-bounds, and the failure path frees safely. Only benign input-validation gaps remain (e.g., nb_sectors and a non-zero-but-negative tracks value are stored without upper-bound checks and can cause issues only in other, out-of-scope consumers).

evidence.reason: The bounds check caps catalog_size so catalog_size*4 cannot overflow (max 2,147,483,644), ensuring g_malloc and the subsequent bdrv_pread of the same size are consistent and the classic heap-overflow-from-integer-overflow is not reachable.
Header is read into a fixed-size stack struct with a full-size read that fails on short read/error; magic, version, and tracks are validated before the catalog is processed.

Catalog buffer is allocated at exactly the read size, reads are error-checked, and the endian-conversion loop is bounded by the same catalog_size, so all writes to catalog_bitmap stay within the allocation.

assumptions: catalog_size is an unsigned 32-bit field in BDRVParallelsState; with that type the INT_MAX/4 guard fully blocks the multiplication overflow.
bdrv_pread returns 0 on success and a negative error on failure/short read, so partially initialized buffers are not used.
bs->opaque is zero-initialized, so g_free(s->catalog_bitmap) on early failure paths is a NULL free.
g_malloc aborts on allocation failure (QEMU convention), so an extreme-but-allowed catalog only risks a crash/DoS, not corruption.
limitations: Analysis is limited to parallels_open; nb_sectors and tracks are stored without upper-bound validation, and their effect on other driver functions (read/write paths) is not evaluated here.

verdict.summary: The GBR brush loader computes pixel buffer sizes with 32-bit unsigned arithmetic (size = width*height*bytes), while the sanitizer boundary check uses 64-bit G_MAXSIZE division. Large attacker-controlled width/height/bytes values overrun 32 bits, produce a wrapped (undersized) allocation, and subsequent loops in the case 1 (.gpb pattern) and case 2 (16-bit float) branches write/read far beyond the heap buffer. The non-NUL-terminated name buffer passed to gimp_any_to_utf8 with length -1 is an additional out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: bh.width/bh.height/bh.bytes are guint32; the multiplication wraps modulo 2^32 before widening to gsize. The sanitizer above accepts products up to G_MAXSIZE (2^64-1), so e.g. 65536*65536*1 passes the check but yields size=0, allocating a buffer far smaller than the declared image.

if ((bh.width == 0) || (bh.width > GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE) ||

Allocation size, loop bound, and index all use 32-bit multiplications that can wrap. With wrapped values the loop writes 4 bytes per iteration past the allocation (CWE-787) and reads plain_brush[i] out of bounds (CWE-125).

With bytes=2 and a wrapped size (e.g. width=height=100000), the loop iterates width*height times over a buffer that only holds the wrapped size, causing out-of-bounds reads via *buf and out-of-bounds writes via brush_buf[i].

verdict.summary: In search_impl, a successful backward search computes the post-match remainder length as count + size - 1, where count equals the match start offset p. This can be far larger than the actual remaining bytes (and size - 1 underflows for empty patterns), producing a string object whose declared length exceeds its buffer. Subsequent accesses to that pushed string read out of bounds, enabling memory disclosure or crashes on crafted input; reaching the backward path depends on the caller's forward flag.

evidence.snippet:
op1->value.bytes = ptr + size;
    r_set_size(op1, count + (!forward ? (size - 1) : 0));
evidence.reason: For !forward, after a match at offset p, count equals p, so the set length is p + size - 1 instead of the true remaining length count0 - p. Example: target "ab", pattern "b" yields a 1-byte string starting at offset 2, past the buffer end; target "abcde", pattern "cde" yields a 4-byte string starting at offset 5. The over-length string is pushed via make_true(op), so later reads are out of bounds. Additionally, when size == 0 and !forward, (size - 1) wraps to UINT_MAX, and count + UINT_MAX wraps to an enormous length.

The scan loop itself is bounds-safe: it executes count0 + 1 times, testing positions 0..count0 forward and count0..0 backward, and all pattern comparisons stay within the target buffer. However, the loop's post-condition on count feeds the flawed length computation at the found label: for backward searches, count is decremented only for failed iterations, leaving count equal to p (match offset), which is then misused as a length.

assumptions: r_size/r_set_size operate on 32-bit unsigned ints and value.bytes points into a contiguous buffer of r_size bytes.
The operands are untrusted string objects supplied through the interpreter's operand stack.
The forward == false path is reachable via some caller of search_impl; reachability from user-controlled PostScript was not verifiable from this snippet alone.
Line numbers are approximate, derived from the provided snippet layout.
limitations: Only the given function body was analyzed; surrounding definitions (check_read_type, make_false/make_true, push, r_size/r_set_size) were not inspected.
Whether the over-length string is subsequently dereferenced depends on the PostScript operators invoked after search, which are outside this snippet.

verdict.summary: No memory-safety vulnerability is demonstrable in the given code. dev_alloc_skb(MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE) reserves NET_SKB_PAD headroom and exposes at least MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE writable bytes at skb->data, so memset(skb->data, 0, MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE) is in-bounds. Because skb->len is 0 at the alignment step, skb_pull(skb, 64 - dword_align_bytes) returns NULL and changes nothing, making the 64-byte alignment branch effectively dead logic (a functional weakness, not memory unsafety in this snippet). Error handling frees the skb exactly once; no double-free or UAF is visible. Residual risk depends on out-of-scope rsi_prepare_beacon internals and the tx_queue array bounds.

evidence.reason: dev_alloc_skb(X) provides at least X bytes of linear data at skb->data after NET_SKB_PAD headroom; the memset of exactly X bytes ends at or before skb->end and stays within the allocation. The NULL check prevents a NULL dereference.

evidence.snippet: dword_align_bytes = ((unsigned long)skb->data & 0x3f); if (dword_align_bytes) skb_pull(skb, (64 - dword_align_bytes));
evidence.reason: skb->len is 0 at this point, so skb_pull's len > skb->len guard triggers and the call returns NULL without moving skb->data or changing skb->len. The alignment logic never takes effect; no pointer moves toward skb->end within this snippet.

evidence.snippet: if (rsi_prepare_beacon(common, skb)) { rsi_dbg(ERR_ZONE, "Failed to prepare beacon\n"); dev_kfree_skb(skb); return -EINVAL; } skb_queue_tail(&common->tx_queue[MGMT_BEACON_Q], skb);
evidence.reason: On failure the skb is freed once and never queued (no double-free). On success ownership is transferred to the queue. rsi_prepare_beacon's internal frame writes and the tx_queue[MGMT_BEACON_Q] bounds are outside the provided code and cannot be validated here.

assumptions: Standard Linux networking semantics hold: dev_alloc_skb(X) reserves NET_SKB_PAD headroom and exposes at least X writable payload bytes at skb->data.
skb->len is 0 immediately after dev_alloc_skb, so the alignment skb_pull is a no-op.

limitations: rsi_prepare_beacon's implementation is not provided; memory-safety issues could exist in its frame-building code.
Array bounds of common->tx_queue[] cannot be verified from this snippet.

verdict.summary: bgp_capability_msg_parse has a heap out-of-bounds read: the loop guarantees only 3 bytes (action/code/length) before memcpy copies sizeof(struct capability) bytes (larger than 3), overreading past the end of the message buffer. verdict.summary: In the per-channel branch, gradient/input/backprop are reshaped with flat_inner_outer_dims<T,3>(axis_ - 1), making the middle (channel) dimension dims[axis_-1] while all validated sizes (depth, min/max tensor sizes, min/max backprop allocations) are based on dims[axis_]. When dims[axis_-1] > dims[axis_], the functor's channel loop reads and writes past the depth-sized min/max inputs and backprop buffers (heap OOB read/write). Additionally, the explicitly allowed axis_ == 0 produces a negative start index (-1) into the shape's dimension array, and scalar/empty min/max tensors are not rejected in all paths, permitting one-element scalar/vec views over zero- or one-element buffers that are then indexed up to depth.

evidence.snippet:
gradient.template flat_inner_outer_dims<T, 3>(axis_ - 1),
 input.template flat_inner_outer_dims<T, 3>(axis_ - 1),
 &input_min_tensor, &input_max_tensor,
 input_backprop->template flat_inner_outer_dims<T, 3>(axis_ - 1),
evidence.reason: Per-channel views use axis_ - 1 as the start, so the middle dimension is dims[axis_-1], not the validated depth = dims[axis_]. The functor's per-channel indexing then exceeds the depth-sized min/max input vectors and min/max backprop buffers when dims[axis_-1] > dims[axis_], causing heap OOB read (CWE-125) and write (CWE-787). For axis_ == 0 the start is -1, an out-of-range dimension index.

For a 0-dim (scalar) min/max tensor with axis_ != -1, dim_size(0) indexes dimension 0 of a shape with 0 dims (CHECK abort in debug, out-of-range dims read in release). If the comparison accidentally passes, the per-channel functor treats the 1-element scalar buffer as a depth-element vector, yielding an OOB read.

The one-scale branch performs no size check on min/max. A shape [0] (empty, dims==1) min or max tensor passes the dims()==1 check; scalar<T>() then reads one element from a zero-element buffer (OOB read), and vectors larger than 1 element are also silently accepted.

assumptions: Eigen's flat_inner_outer_dims<T,3>(start) produces a 3-D view whose middle dimension is dims[start], with outer and inner dims formed by products of the remaining ranges.
Release builds disable DCHECK-style bounds checks (NDEBUG), so out-of-range dimension indexing and tensor-view accesses proceed as raw memory accesses.
The per-channel gradient functor derives its channel index from the reshaped middle dimension and indexes the min/max input tensors and flat min/max backprop buffers by that channel.
limitations: The exact TensorShape::dim_size behavior for an out-of-range index (wrap, return 0, or raw OOB read) depends on the TensorFlow version; the analysis covers the dangerous cases in each interpretation.

The code sample omits the functor implementations and Eigen view internals, so precise overflow conditions (e.g., exact index formula) are inferred from the validated depth contract rather than observed.
Whether an OOB is reached depends on attacker-controlled tensor shapes/axis satisfying dims[axis_-1] > dims[axis_]; other shapes only cause incorrect results.

verdict.summary: thread_call ignores the return value of sq_reservestack and then unconditionally pushes the roottable plus nparams-1 arguments onto the target thread. sq_reservestack can fail (e.g., allocation failure or exceeding the thread stack size limit) and leave the underlying buffer unchanged or undersized.
stack_get(v,1) is valid for native calls because the VM always pushes a receiver, so no out-of-bounds read was assumed there.
limitations: Exact line numbers and the thread stack layout are inferred from Squirrel's base library implementation; the caller could not verify the surrounding VM internals.

verdict.summary: In the NFT_JUMP/NFT_GOTO path, chain->use is incremented without an overflow check. Insufficient input validation (CWE-20): any verdict code whose low 8 bits equal NF_ACCEPT/NF_DROP/NF_QUEUE passes even with arbitrary high bits, and supplying both NFTA_VERDICT_CHAIN and NFTA_VERDICT_CHAIN_ID is silently resolved in favor of the name rather than rejected, leaving attacker-controlled ambiguity in verdict interpretation.

verdict.summary: The newstyle option-negotiation parser validates every attacker-controlled length before allocation/use: optlen is capped by MAX_REQUEST_SIZE before malloc(optlen+1), INFO/GO payloads are checked for exact size before indexed accesses, meta-context reads are guarded by opt_index bounds checks, and num-queries/info loops are bounded by the payload size. verdict.summary: get_recurse_data_length walks the compiled opcode stream trusting embedded length and PRIVATE_DATA fields without bounds validation. The OP_KET branch advances cc via PRIVATE_DATA(cc+1) without checking it stays within [cc, ccend]; a negative value can re-scan/re-loop and overflow the int 'length', while an oversized value skips opcodes. Multi-byte reads (GET2/GET) and the OP_MARK name-length advance can also read past ccend. A too-small returned length makes callers under-allocate recurse-data buffers, enabling a downstream heap overflow.

evidence.reason: Unchecked indirect advance via PRIVATE_DATA(cc+1): an oversized value skips past ccend (assertion is debug-only), while a negative value moves cc backward, re-scanning opcodes, repeatedly incrementing 'length', and risking an unbounded loop plus int overflow.
The embedded 8-bit length cc[1] is trusted without verifying that cc[1] + 3 bytes remain before ccend, allowing the walker to skip past the opcode buffer and return an incorrect word count.
Multi-byte opcode fields (GET2 at 1+LINK_SIZE, GET at 1) are read with only the loop guard cc < ccend, so a field straddling or beyond ccend is an out-of-bounds read.

All accounting uses unchecked int arithmetic; combined with the backward OP_KET jump (re-scan path), 'length' can overflow. The caller uses the return value to size recurse-data buffers, so an under-count leads to undersized allocation and a subsequent heap buffer overflow when the data is written.

assumptions: This function runs during JIT compilation on an opcode stream derived from a user-supplied regular expression.
SLJIT_ASSERT is a no-op in release builds, so the cc == ccend invariant is not enforced at runtime.
The caller allocates/computes recurse-data storage sized from the returned length; an under-count is exploitable downstream.
limitations: PRIVATE_DATA, recurse_check_bit, next_opcode, and the exact caller allocation logic are not shown, so end-to-end exploitability could not be fully verified.

verdict.summary: reserve_sfa_size computes req_size = NLA_ALIGN(attr_len) from an unvalidated int and mixes signed (int) with unsigned (size_t) arithmetic when sizing the action buffer. verdict.summary: do_put() derives int sizes from size_t string lengths and uses an unbounded repetition count. The block-insert and single-line MCHAR paths have explicit multiplication-overflow guards, but the multi-line MCHAR path (y_size > 1) does not: totlen/yanklen are truncated to int from STRLEN(), then alloc(STRLEN(ptr) + totlen + 1) is followed by STRCPY/STRCAT and alloc(col + yanklen + 1) with memmove of yanklen+1, so oversized register lines or columns near INT_MAX produce undersized heap allocations and heap buffer overflows; additionally a large count drives an unbounded line-append loop (resource exhaustion).

evidence.snippet: for (cnt = 1; cnt <= count; ++cnt) { i = 0; if (y_type == MCHAR) { lnum = new_cursor.lnum; ptr = ml_get(lnum) + col; totlen = (int)STRLEN(y_array[y_size - 1]); newp = alloc(STRLEN(ptr) + totlen + 1); if (newp == NULL) goto error; STRCPY(newp, y_array[y_size - 1]); STRCAT(newp, ptr); ... oldp = ml_get(lnum); newp = alloc(col + yanklen + 1); ... mch_memmove(newp + col, y_array[0], (size_t)(yanklen + 1)); }
evidence.reason: Unlike the MBLOCK and MCHAR-y_size==1 paths, this branch has no multiplication/size overflow check. STRLEN() values are narrowed to int (totlen, yanklen) or summed in int (col + yanklen + 1) for the allocation, while STRCPY/STRCAT and memmove later copy the full untruncated lengths; register lines/columns at or above INT_MAX produce undersized allocations followed by heap buffer overflows.

The guard protects ordinary values, but the guard operands (yanklen + spaces) and (bd.startspaces + bd.endspaces) are themselves int expressions that can wrap for oversized register lines, y_width, or virtual columns; after such a wrap the check can pass while totlen no longer bounds the per-row memmoves, enabling heap overflow.

evidence.snippet: for (cnt = 1; cnt <= count; ++cnt) { ... if (ml_append(lnum, y_array[i], (colnr_T)0, FALSE) == FAIL) goto error; ... lnum++; ++nr_lines; ... }
evidence.reason: count is a long used directly as an unbounded loop bound (up to LONG_MAX); each iteration appends or splits lines, so an attacker-influenced count causes uncontrolled memory and CPU consumption (CWE-400), even though allocation/append failures exit gracefully via goto error.

assumptions: count is attacker-influencable up to LONG_MAX (e.g., large command counts or expression-register-driven put)
y_array lines and buffer lines are NUL-terminated C strings, as stored by the yank/register machinery
int/colnr_T are 32-bit on the analyzed target
limitations: Triggering the heap-overflow paths requires register lines, y_width, or virtual columns at or above INT_MAX bytes, which is impractical in most configurations; realistic impact is primarily resource exhaustion from very large counts
The classic MBLOCK and single-line MCHAR multiplication overflows appear already patched in this snapshot; the residual risk is in the multi-line MCHAR path and wrap of the guard arithmetic itself
Reachability of specific count values and virtual-editing states from callers outside this function could not be verified from the provided code alone

verdict.summary: Heap buffer overflow in unix_expandpath(): directory entry names from readdir() are copied with STRCPY into a heap buffer that only reserves BASENAMELEN+5 bytes for the file name component, with no length or capacity check; appending the remaining path suffix can likewise exceed the allocation when the entry name is longer than the wildcard component it replaces. limitations: Analysis is static, based only on the provided snippet; the exact values of BASENAMELEN/NAME_MAX for the target platform are not visible.

verdict.summary: No exploitable security vulnerability found in iwl_trans_pcie_alloc. Error paths free allocated resources exactly once (free_percpu is NULL-safe when the per-CPU page allocation failed; iwl_pcie_free_ict is called only on the ICT path after a successful allocation), MMIO accesses occur only after hw_base is validated non-NULL, the DMA-mask fallback logic is exhaustive, and the hw_id/CSR manipulations use bounded formats and well-defined unsigned operations. Only low-severity robustness gaps exist: unchecked return values of pci_set_master, pci_write_config_byte, pci_disable_link_state, iwl_pcie_set_interrupt_capa, and alloc_workqueue (a NULL workqueue would stall RX allocation under memory pressure, not corrupt memory), plus an implicit assumption that cfg_trans->base_params is non-NULL.

evidence.reason: Size-bounded formatting with %04X matching 16-bit inputs; maximum output ~22 chars plus NUL, so no buffer overflow.
Each error branch reaches cleanup exactly once and returns immediately; free_percpu(NULL) is a safe no-op when tso_hdr_page was never allocated, so no double-free or use-after-free.

DMA mask selection is exhaustive with a 32-bit fallback and a clean error exit if both attempts fail; no DMA is issued before a mask is established.

Unchecked returns for pci_set_master, pci_write_config_byte, pci_disable_link_state, iwl_pcie_set_interrupt_capa, and alloc_workqueue are robustness issues (possible RX-allocator stall if the workqueue is NULL) but do not lead to memory unsafety or privilege escalation in the shown code.

assumptions: iwl_trans_alloc zero-initializes the transport structure, so fields like msix_enabled are not read uninitialized.
cfg_trans/base_params are kernel-supplied constant PCI device configuration data with no system- or user-controlled input path.
Helper functions (iwl_pcie_set_interrupt_capa, iwl_pcie_free_ict, iwl_trans_free) behave as per their kernel contracts.

verdict.summary: mouse_col from external mouse input is used to index TabPageIdxs in the tab-line drag branches without the bounds check that protects the click branch, enabling an out-of-bounds read; a secondary EOF-overrun risk exists in the whitespace-skip loop for double-click word selection, and count is passed unchecked into paste operations.

evidence.reason: TabPageIdxs[mouse_col] is indexed without validating that mouse_col is in range, unlike the is_click path which checks 'mouse_col < Columns' before the same indexing. mouse_col is derived from untrusted terminal/GUI mouse input, so a negative or too-large value yields an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125/CWE-129).

Second unguarded TabPageIdxs[mouse_col] access on the drag path; no upper or lower bound check on mouse_col exists at this point, so the out-of-bounds read is reachable via drag events in the tab line.

inc() is applied without an end-of-file guard while the current buffer tail is whitespace; end_visual can advance past the last line, and the subsequent gchar_pos()/vim_iswordc() calls read an out-of-range position. Whether this is a memory fault depends on clamping inside the unshown gchar_pos/ml_get helpers (medium-low confidence).

assumptions: mouse_col and mouse_row are populated from external mouse input and are not guaranteed to be within the tab-line / Columns range merely by the caller.
Line numbers are approximate, counted relative to the top of the provided snippet.
Helper behavior (gchar_pos, inc, ml_get, jump_to_mouse, mouse_has) was not shown and was assumed to be the standard Vim implementation.
limitations: The out-of-bounds read via TabPageIdxs is confirmed by control-flow comparison of the guarded click path vs. the unguarded drag paths, but actual exploitability (crash vs. logic-only) depends on the runtime layout of TabPageIdxs.
The whitespace-skip loop's memory effect could not be confirmed without the internals of gchar_pos/ml_get clamping.
Integer-overflow candidates in the block-visual corner math are noted but judged low severity given practical bounds on line/column numbers.

verdict.summary: No exploitable vulnerability found in the provided function. All arithmetic that could divide by zero is guarded by early-return checks (numRecords > 100 on the non-timeseries trial path; numRecords != 0 plus bucketUnpacker present on the timeseries path), arithmetic is done in double so long long counts cannot overflow, and the raw trialStage pointer observed after std::move(root) remains owned by the created PlanExecutor and is never dereferenced on the error path.

evidence.snippet: if (sampleSize > numRecords * kMaxSampleRatioForRandCursor || numRecords <= 100) { return std::pair{nullptr, false}; }
evidence.reason: Guarantees numRecords > 100 before the sharded trial path, so sampleSize / (numRecords * 0.05) always has a non-zero, positive denominator; the multiplication is promoted to double, preventing integer overflow.

evidence.snippet: if (!(bucketUnpacker && numRecords)) { return std::pair{nullptr, false}; } ... const auto minAdvancedToWorkRatio = std::max(std::min(sampleSize / (kCoefficient * numRecords * gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount), 1.0), kMinBucketFullness);
evidence.reason: The (bucketUnpacker && numRecords) guard prevents the empty-collection NaN/division-by-zero case; the subsequent division and clamping keep the ratio finite, and all arithmetic is floating-point.

evidence.snippet: auto execStatus = plan_executor_factory::make(...); if (!execStatus.isOK()) { return execStatus.getStatus(); } return std::pair{std::move(execStatus.getValue()), !trialStage || !trialStage->pickedBackupPlan()};
evidence.reason: trialStage aliases the object previously owned by root; after std::move(root) the executor retains ownership so the pointer stays valid, and the error path returns before any dereference, so no use-after-free is reachable.

assumptions: Callers guarantee expCtx and coll pointers are valid and the MODE_IS collection lock is held before entry.
Upstream callers validate that the $sample size is a non-negative long long and numRecords is a non-negative collection count.
gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount is a server parameter whose validation keeps it above zero.
Trusted components outside this function (TrialStage, SampleFromTimeseriesBucket, CollectionScan, storage-engine random cursor) are not analyzed here.
limitations: Static analysis only; no runtime input profiling or fuzzing was performed.
Floating-point comparisons with long long counts near 9.2e18 could lose precision in theory, but the early-return ratio bounds make this non-exploitable on reachable paths.

If gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount could be configured to 0, the timeseries ratio could become NaN/inf and degrade plan selection (an availability edge case), but this is not memory-unsafe and appears constrained by parameter validation.

verdict.summary: In the ':filter' modifier handling, skip_vimgrep_pat_ext() inserts a NUL byte into the command buffer to terminate the pattern; the original byte is restored only after vim_regcomp() succeeds. assumptions: eap->cmd points to a NUL-terminated writable buffer at entry.
checkforcmd_noparen/checkforcmd_opt advance eap->cmd only on a successful keyword match.
The visual-range rewriting arithmetic was verified against buffer capacity and is in-bounds for all reachable modifier lengths.
limitations: No out-of-bounds read/write or use-after-free could be proven from this function in isolation.
Assignments like eap->cmd = (char_u *)"'<,'>+" hand a string literal to callers; whether downstream code mutates eap->cmd is outside this snippet.
Exact line numbers were not provided, so evidence locations are null.
The precise CVE mapping (if any) for this defect could not be verified from the code alone.

verdict.summary: A crafted squashfs image can trigger (1) a stack buffer overflow because dire->size is a signed short and the >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN check does not reject negative values, so memcpy(dire->name, ..., dire->size + 1) uses a huge size_t length writing past the stack buffer and reading past directory_table; (2) out-of-bounds heap reads of directory_table because header/entry/name reads are never bounded by the table length and the loop bound size is derived from attacker-controlled inode fields; and (3) a use-after-free because the corrupted path frees dir and then returns the dangling pointer.

evidence.reason: dire->size is a signed short; negative sizes (e.g., 0xFFFE) bypass the length check, then memcpy's size argument dire->size + 1 converts to a near-maximum size_t, overflowing the fixed stack buffer 'buffer' and over-reading directory_table. The index dire->size + 1 also becomes negative for sizes < -1, writing before dire->name.

All reads from directory_table are at unvalidated offsets: bytes is never checked against the actual table allocation, and the loop bound size = (*i)->data + bytes - 3 is derived from attacker-controlled inode fields. No check ensures sizeof(dirh), sizeof(*dire), or dire->size + 1 bytes remain, enabling heap over-reads.
The corrupted path frees dir and dir->dirs but then returns the freed dir pointer; callers dereference the result, causing a use-after-free.

assumptions: struct squashfs_dir_entry's size field is a signed 16-bit short, as in squashfs-tools, making the >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN check insufficient against negative values.
directory_table is a heap buffer decompressed from the image whose real length is not validated against the attacker-controlled loop bound.
Line numbers are unknown because the file was provided without a path or line markers.
limitations: The analysis is based only on the supplied code; callers' subsequent handling of the returned dangling pointer could not be inspected.
Exact triggerability of each issue depends on squashfs-tools' struct layout and the endian-swap macros, which are not shown here.

verdict.summary: The EDID read index is derived as s->reg % sizeof(s->edid_blob), where sizeof yields an unsigned size_t. Usual arithmetic conversions confine the resulting index to [0, N-1] for every possible reg value, including negative signed values, so no out-of-bounds read is reachable in this code. Only low-severity robustness concerns remain: reg is incremented without an explicit upper check (covered by the modulo), and a signed-char edid_blob would sign-extend bytes >= 0x80 into negative int return values, which is a correctness issue rather than a memory-safety one.

evidence.snippet: value = s->edid_blob[s->reg % sizeof(s->edid_blob)];
evidence.reason: The modulo operand is sizeof(...), i.e. an unsigned size_t N. Per C usual arithmetic conversions, any signed reg is converted to unsigned before the operation, and the result always lies in [0, N-1]; a negative reg cannot produce a negative index or an index >= N. The read is therefore in-bounds on every path.

evidence.snippet: s->reg++;
evidence.reason: reg grows without bound, but the modulo operation keeps all subsequent indices valid. Signed overflow of the counter would be undefined behavior only after an impractical ~2^31 increments and still cannot lead to an out-of-bounds access, so this is a robustness nuance rather than an exploitable flaw here.

assumptions: s->edid_blob is declared as an array member so sizeof yields its full byte length (not a pointer size).
s->reg is an integer type (e.g., int, uint8_t, or uint16_t); other integer-like types do not change the modulo bounds due to the size_t operand.
Access is not concurrent; data races on s->reg are out of scope for this snippet.
The caller passes a valid I2CSlave whose object actually is an I2CDDCState, so the container_of cast is safe.
limitations: The struct definition for I2CDDCState and the callers that set s->reg are not shown, so the element type of edid_blob (signed char vs uint8_t) and how reg is initialized/written by bus traffic could not be verified directly.
Only one-byte array reads are analyzed; other handlers (write path) that may set reg are not visible here.

verdict.summary: No confirmed buffer overflow: the local-data buffer is exactly sized and the rrlen-1 margins keep every snprintf write in bounds, but in the all-escaped worst case the trailing quote is silently truncated, producing a malformed TXT local-data entry (CWE-130). Additional low-severity issues: unchecked strdup() results can insert NULL entries leading to NULL dereference on memory exhaustion (CWE-476); a fixed 4-byte memcpy from cert->serial with no verified field-size bound is a potential heap over-read pending the struct definition (CWE-125); the whole struct including padding is serialized, potentially disclosing uninitialized bytes; rrlen is uint16_t and truncates for very long provider names.

evidence.snippet: rrlen = strlen(dnscenv->provider_name) + strlen(ttl_class_type) + 4 * sizeof(struct SignedCert) + 1 + 1; rr = malloc(rrlen);
evidence.reason: rrlen is uint16_t, so a provider_name longer than ~65529 bytes truncates the computed size; writes stay bound to the truncated size, so the effect is truncated/malformed output rather than overflow, but the length handling is fragile (CWE-130).

evidence.snippet: snprintf(rr, rrlen - 1, "%s 86400 IN TXT \"", dnscenv->provider_name); ... snprintf(rr + strlen(rr), rrlen - 1 - strlen(rr), "\"");
evidence.reason: All writes use rrlen-1 margins, guaranteeing strlen(rr) <= rrlen-2 and in-bounds writes; however, when every certificate byte escapes to 4 characters, the final quote write gets size 1 and drops the quote, inserting malformed zone text into cfg->local_data (CWE-130).

evidence.snippet: memcpy(&serial, cert->serial, sizeof serial); serial = htonl(serial);
evidence.reason: Unconditionally copies 4 bytes from cert->serial without validating the member size; if serial is shorter than 4 bytes this is an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125). Requires struct SignedCert layout to confirm; assumed 4-byte array here.

evidence.snippet: cfg_strlist_insert(&cfg->local_data, strdup(rr));
evidence.reason: strdup() return is unchecked; on OOM a NULL entry is inserted and later dereferenced by the config parser (CWE-476/CWE-252). The same unchecked-strdup pattern appears in the local-zone insert at lines 5-7, which also leaks both strings on failure (CWE-401).

evidence.snippet: for(j=0; j<sizeof(struct SignedCert); j++){ int c = (int)*((const uint8_t *) cert + j); ... snprintf(rr + strlen(rr), rrlen - 1 - strlen(rr), "\\%03d", c); }
evidence.reason: Serializes the entire struct including padding and any uninitialized fields into a DNS TXT record and verbose logs; if the struct is not fully initialized, heap bytes are potentially disclosed (CWE-665/CWE-200). Worst-case escape cost is 4 bytes/struct byte, matching the sizing; no overflow.

assumptions: struct SignedCert is not defined in the snippet; cert->serial is assumed to be at least 4 bytes (e.g., uint8_t serial[4]).
dnscenv->signed_certs and dnscenv->rotated_certs are assumed to be valid, correctly sized arrays; rotated_certs entries are assumed to point into the signed_certs array for the pointer comparison.
provider_name, cert bytes, and config are assumed to come from operator/provider-controlled sources (not attacker-controlled network input).
isprint() is assumed to operate on the valid unsigned-char range since c is derived from uint8_t.
limitations: Base reasoning is limited to this function; caller context, struct definitions, and the behaviors of cfg_str2list_insert/cfg_strlist_insert are not visible.
The memory-safety analysis relies on the exact-fit arithmetic in this snippet; any change to the size formula or removal of the -1 margins could introduce an overflow.
Uninitialized-padding disclosure and the cert->serial over-read could not be confirmed without the struct definition and allocation/initialization site.

verdict.summary: The function indexes fm->hdf[u] and fm->hd[u] with caller-supplied u without any upper-bounds check; the only guard (u < HTTP_HDR_FIRST) executes after the first array read and only tests the lower end. Out-of-range u causes out-of-bounds reads, and the filter bit is consulted before the header-type guard, which can also yield incorrect filtering decisions.
