if (fm->hdf[u] & HDF_FILTER)
		return (1);
evidence.reason: fm->hdf[u] is dereferenced with unvalidated u before the u < HTTP_HDR_FIRST check on line 8; there is no upper-bound check, so u outside the hdf/hd array bounds causes an out-of-bounds read that the later guard cannot prevent.

fm->hd[u].b is indexed with the same unvalidated u (second out-of-bounds read path), and strchr scans until ':' or NUL, requiring a NUL-terminated buffer and risking an over-read if that invariant is not upheld for the header slot.

assumptions: hdf and hd are fixed-size parallel arrays in struct http, so an out-of-range u affects both.
Header buffers are expected to be NUL-terminated by surrounding invariants.
The filter decision for invalid u values is treated as security-relevant because this function gates header filtering.
limitations: The exact array size (HDRS or fm->nhd) is not visible in the snippet, so the precise trigger range for the out-of-bounds read is unknown.
Whether u can be attacker-controlled depends on callers, which are not shown.
The function is analyzed in isolation; surrounding invariant enforcement (e.g., asserts, caller-side validation) may mitigate the flaw in practice.

verdict.summary: No memory-safety or input-validation vulnerability found in win_redr_status in the provided code. All NameBuff writes are bounded by MAXPATHL via vim_snprintf with remaining-size checks and truncation math that stays in-bounds; column arithmetic is clamped; the reentrancy guard is reset on all paths. The multibyte truncation path overwrites the final byte of a multibyte character, causing only display corruption, not an out-of-bounds access. Residual risk depends on unseen callees (get_trans_bufname, mb_ptr2len, screen_puts, win_redr_ruler).

evidence.snippet: vim_snprintf((char *)p + len, MAXPATHL - len, "%s", _("[Help]")); len += (int)STRLEN(p + len);
evidence.reason: Every suffix append passes the remaining buffer size MAXPATHL - len to an snprintf-style formatter; the size arithmetic keeps len at most MAXPATHL - 1, so writes stay within NameBuff. The space append is additionally gated by len < MAXPATHL - 1.

evidence.snippet: for (i = 0; p[i] != NUL && clen >= this_ru_col - 1; i += (*mb_ptr2len)(p + i)) ... if (i > 0) { p = p + i - 1; *p = '<'; ++len; }
evidence.reason: The loop terminates at the NUL terminator, so i is bounded by the string length and p + i - 1 points inside NameBuff when i > 0. The write replaces one byte of a multibyte character (display-only corruption), not an out-of-bounds address. Column arithmetic is clamped to at least (w_width + 1) / 2 before use.

evidence.snippet: if (busy) return; busy = TRUE; ... busy = FALSE;
evidence.reason: The only early return occurs before busy is set, and no other return exists after busy = TRUE, so recursive invocations are safely ignored and the flag is always restored.

assumptions: NameBuff is at least MAXPATHL bytes and NUL-terminated after get_trans_bufname()
get_trans_bufname() itself writes no more than MAXPATHL - 1 bytes into NameBuff
mb_ptr2len() does not read beyond the NUL terminator of the string
wp->w_width is at least 1 and ru_col/Columns are valid screen columns
screen_puts, screen_fill and win_redr_ruler clamp output to the screen bounds
limitations: Callee implementations (redraw_custom_statusline, get_trans_bufname, mb_string2cells, mb_ptr2len, screen_puts, fillchar_status, win_redr_ruler) are not part of the provided code and could introduce their own defects
FEAT_* compile-time branches are analyzed statically only for the code shown
The single-byte write *p = '<' in the multibyte path can produce invalid UTF-8 display output, which is a correctness/robustness issue rather than a memory-safety vulnerability

verdict.summary: ST21NFCA connectivity EVT_TRANSACTION handling trusts attacker-controlled skb data: the length/tag validation uses '&&' instead of '||' and lacks any skb->len bounds checks, 'transaction->aid_len' (0-255) is copied into a 16-byte aid field inside an allocation of only 'skb->len - 2' bytes (heap out-of-bounds write, possible 'skb->len - 2' unsigned underflow), and subsequent index reads/copies (data[aid_len+2], data[aid_len+3], data+aid_len+4) perform out-of-bounds reads of the skb.

evidence.reason: Logical-AND instead of logical-OR: the guard is bypassed when the buffer is long enough OR when the first byte is the AID tag, allowing short/malformed buffers through; also dereferences skb->data[0] without checking skb->len >= 1.
Allocation size is attacker-controlled 'skb->len - 2', smaller than 'struct nfc_evt_transaction'; if skb->len < 2 the unsigned subtraction wraps to a huge size (CWE-190).

Unchecked aid_len (0-255) copied into a 16-byte aid field within an undersized allocation: heap out-of-bounds write past the kmalloc'd buffer; source and skb->data[1] reads also out of bounds when skb->len is short.
Index 'aid_len + 2' is never checked against skb->len, so the tag read is an out-of-bounds read whose value influences control flow.
Params index read and memcpy source span (aid_len+4 .. +4+params_len) are unchecked against skb->len; both are out-of-bounds reads, and the write still targets the undersized allocation.

assumptions: 'struct nfc_evt_transaction' contains fixed-size 'aid'/'params' arrays (<= 16 / 255 bytes per the ETSI 102 622 table referenced in the comment) and 'skb->len' is unsigned.
skb data at EVT_TRANSACTION is attacker-influenced (malicious NFC peer/controller can craft the event payload).
limitations: Exact line numbers are approximate relative to the supplied snippet; 'NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH'/'NFC_MAX_AID_LENGTH' values (default 5/16) are inferred from the referenced ETSI table.
Reachability depends on the NFC stack delivering an ST21NFCA_EVT_TRANSACTION event; exploitation generally requires NFC proximity or control of the NFC controller.
Post-allocation '-EPROTO' returns leak the devm-allocated transaction until device teardown; this is a secondary DoS issue, not the primary overflow.

verdict.summary: NULL pointer dereference in inflate()'s gzip EXTRA-field handling: `len = state->head->extra_len - state->length;` executes before the `state->head != Z_NULL` check, so a crafted gzip stream with FEXTRA (0x0400) and nonzero XLEN dereferences a NULL state->head when the application never called inflateGetHeader(), causing a crash (denial of service). In canonical zlib this assignment is inside the guard's short-circuit condition.

evidence.reason: The expression `state->head->extra_len` dereferences `state->head` unconditionally whenever a nonzero amount of extra-field data is available, before the subsequent NULL check. With gzip support enabled (GUNZIP), `state->flags` and `state->length` come directly from attacker-controlled header bytes (FLAGS/EXLEN), and `state->head` remains NULL unless the application registered a gzip header via inflateGetHeader(). A malicious stream with the FEXTRA flag and a nonzero XLEN therefore reaches this line and crashes the process.

assumptions: Gzip support is compiled in (GUNZIP defined), which is the default in zlib.
The calling application does not call inflateGetHeader(), leaving `state->head == Z_NULL`.
The attacker can supply gzip-compressed input to inflate() with wrap mode allowing gzip headers (wrap & 2).
Line numbers are approximate, derived from the provided excerpt without original line numbering.
limitations: Only the provided source excerpt was analyzed; `inflate_fast()`, `inflate_table()`, and the macro definitions (NEEDBITS, PULLBYTE, LOAD, RESTORE) were not available for review.
Impact is limited to a NULL pointer dereference (crash/DoS); no memory corruption or code execution was identified in the examined paths.

verdict.summary: No exploitable vulnerability identified. The size cap (size <= RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ) prevents overflow/truncation in len computation, masked indexing keeps all writes within the ring data region, producer access is serialized by a spinlock with a safe NMI trylock path, and unsigned wrap-around in producer-position arithmetic can only cause conservative rejection, never an out-of-bounds write or bypassed space check.

evidence.snippet: if (unlikely(size > RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ)) return NULL; len = round_up(size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, 8); ... if (new_prod_pos - cons_pos > rb->mask) { ... return NULL; }
evidence.reason: The input-cap branch combined with the capacity check prevents integer overflow in `size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ`, prevents u32 truncation of `len`, and rejects records that would exceed ring capacity. Unsigned wrap of `new_prod_pos` can only produce an underflowed difference that exceeds `rb->mask`, leading to a NULL return.

evidence.snippet: hdr = (void *)rb->data + (prod_pos & rb->mask); pg_off = bpf_ringbuf_rec_pg_off(rb, hdr); hdr->len = size | BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT; hdr->pg_off = pg_off; smp_store_release(&rb->producer_pos, new_prod_pos);
evidence.reason: All header writes target addresses derived with `prod_pos & rb->mask`, bounding them to the ring's data region. The release store publishes the header before the producer position advances, pairing correctly with the consumer's acquire load; no out-of-bounds write or memory-ordering flaw is evident.

assumptions: RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ is the kernel's small compile-time constant (well below UINT32_MAX), so `len`'s u32 type cannot truncate the rounded record size.
rb->mask equals the ring data region size minus one, and the ring's data pages are double-mapped so records crossing the virtual end are contiguous in memory.
bpf_ringbuf_rec_pg_off() returns a page offset valid for the ring's page layout.
The caller (bpf_ringbuf_reserve entry point) enforces additional helper permissions/checks outside this snippet.
limitations: Analysis is based only on the provided snippet; surrounding code (ring buffer creation, consumer path, page remapping, helper entry checks) is not shown and was not audited here.
A stale consumer_pos snapshot can cause spurious reservation failures under load, but this is a liveness concern, not a security vulnerability.

verdict.summary: Integer-overflow and unsigned-underflow bugs in reserve_sfa_size(): NLA_ALIGN(attr_len) can become huge when attr_len is negative, next_offset/new_acts_size truncate from size_t to int, ksize(*sfa) - next_offset underflows when next_offset exceeds the allocation size, and actions_len (u32) wraps when adding req_size. These can bypass the MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE cap and cause heap out-of-bounds writes in memcpy or at the returned attribute pointer.

evidence.reason: attr_len is a signed int with no validation: NLA_ALIGN of a negative value stays negative (becoming huge as size_t), and summing the u32 actions_len into an int next_offset can truncate/wrap, producing an invalid negative offset used as the returned write pointer.

evidence.snippet:
if (req_size <= (ksize(*sfa) - next_offset))
	goto out;
evidence.reason: Mixed size_t/int subtraction: if next_offset exceeds ksize(*sfa), the result underflows to a huge size_t, so the 'enough space' check passes and the caller writes req_size bytes at next_offset beyond the live allocation.

evidence.snippet:
new_acts_size = max(next_offset + req_size, ksize(*sfa) * 2);

if (new_acts_size > MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE) {
evidence.reason: next_offset + req_size is computed in size_t then truncated to int new_acts_size; a truncated negative value bypasses the MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE comparison and is later passed to nla_alloc_flow_actions as an invalid size.

evidence.snippet: (*sfa)->actions_len += req_size;
evidence.reason: u32 actions_len is incremented by a size_t req_size without range checking; a large or negative-derived req_size wraps the field, shrinking the recorded length so later space checks under-estimate usage and later writes can go out of bounds.

assumptions: attr_len is ultimately attacker-influenced (e.g., derived from OVS netlink action attribute lengths).
struct sw_flow_actions uses a flexible array member actions[] and ksize() returns the actual kmalloc bucket size; NLA_ALIGN(x) is ((x)+3)&~3.
The function is invoked repeatedly per action attribute, so state (actions_len) carries across calls.
limitations: Only the isolated function was provided; callers are not shown, so exact reachability of negative/huge attr_len or actions_len near INT_MAX/U32_MAX is not fully verified.
In the real kernel, common callers derive attr_len from nla_len (u16), bounding it to ~64KB, which limits direct exploitation unless triggered through accumulated state or another caller.
Line numbers are approximate relative to the snippet; no file/line context was given.

verdict.summary: gopherToHTML() has multiple security flaws reachable from untrusted gopher/CSO server data: an off-by-one out-of-bounds write when NUL-terminating a full-size line (line[llen + 1] with llen == TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1), a NULL-pointer dereference when a menu item has a host but no port (*port on NULL), a varargs format-argument count mismatch in the GOPHER_WWW branch (5 specifiers, 3 arguments), and missing HTML escaping of server-controlled host/port fields that allows attribute/HTML injection into the generated page.

evidence.snippet: line[llen + 1] = '\0';
evidence.reason: When the overflow guard fires, llen is clamped to TEMP_BUF_SIZE - gopherState->len - 1, so for gopherState->len == 0 the terminator write lands at line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE], one byte past the TEMP_BUF_SIZE-sized stack/local array (off-by-one OOB write, CWE-787). A gopher line >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE bytes triggers it.

If a menu line has a host but no third TAB (port == NULL), the code still reaches the output formatting and dereferences port via *port, causing a NULL-pointer dereference / crash on malformed server input (CWE-476).

Memory safety is otherwise sound: allocations are checked and all option writes use bounded strlcat, so the impact is mtab content corruption/spoofing rather than memory corruption.

evidence.reason: User-controlled strings are assigned without validation for newlines or field separators; they are later emitted verbatim by addmntent into the root-owned mtab while CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE is active, enabling mtab record injection.

The passwd-derived username is appended without content validation; a username containing CR/LF can inject options/records, and silent truncation by strlcat can produce malformed 'user=' fields that confuse mtab parsers.

The privileged write to the mtab is performed with CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE enabled and without O_NOFOLLOW; combined with the unvalidated record contents this widens the impact of the injection, and a controlled symlink at MOUNTED could redirect the append.

assumptions: The caller is a privileged mount helper reachable by unprivileged users (e.g., setuid mount flow), so devname/mountpoint are user-influenced.
getusername, lock_mtab, and toggle_dac_capability are trusted helpers returning valid, NUL-terminated strings.

limitations: Callers and any upstream validation of devname/mountpoint/fstype are not part of the provided code.

verdict.summary: The status-line redraw routine appends tokens to the shared NameBuff using a cursor (len = STRLEN(NameBuff)) that is never bounds-checked against MAXPATHL. For a file name that nearly fills the buffer, '*(p + len++) = ' '' can overwrite the NUL terminator and the following STRLEN(p + len) reads past the end of NameBuff (OOB read/UB); if the NameBuff length invariant is broken, the append becomes an OOB write. The static 'busy' reentrancy flag is also left set if control flow is interrupted, permanently disabling status-line redraws.

evidence.reason: No check that len < MAXPATHL before appending. With a near-MAXPATHL-length buffer name, the space write clobbers the NUL terminator at index MAXPATHL-1 and subsequent STRLEN(p + len) (len == MAXPATHL) reads one element past NameBuff (out-of-bounds read / undefined behavior).

The token-append chain trusts the unvalidated len cursor for both the destination pointer and the size argument. If len exceeds MAXPATHL (or the NameBuff length invariant fails), MAXPATHL - len underflows to a huge size_t, enabling an out-of-bounds write; even at len == MAXPATHL the STRLEN(p + len) re-read is out of bounds.

busy is reset only at the normal end of the function. An interrupted path (e.g., longjmp/out-of-memory machinery during drawing) or concurrent invocation leaves busy set, causing a permanent denial-of-service where status lines are never redrawn; it is also not thread-safe.

verdict.summary: get_one_sourceline can fall off the end of a non-void function: when the loop exits without reading data (ga_grow failure, no remaining buflines, fgets returning NULL at EOF/error, or an immediate Ctrl-Z in EOL_DOS mode before have_read is set), the function calls vim_free(ga.ga_data) and returns without a value instead of returning NULL. verdict.summary: In jetp3852_print_page, the transpose loop indexes the 8-element static lookup tables spr40/spr8/spr2 with raw raster bytes (dp[0..7], values 0..255) that are never validated to be <= 7. verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled BMP dimensions flow into size_t multiplications (bytes_per_line = 4*((columns*bpp+31)/32); length = bytes_per_line*rows) and into buffer-size computations (rows*MagickMax(bytes_per_line, columns+256)) with no overflow validation and only a weak length/8 blob-size heuristic. Per-row data consumption (3*columns bytes for 24bpp, 4*columns for 32bpp, columns for 8bpp, 2*columns for 16bpp) only stays within the buffer if the original bytes_per_line did not wrap; on 32-bit overflow only MagickMax(bytes_per_line, columns+256) bounds the allocation, so rows near the top read/write beyond the end of the heap buffer (CWE-787).

The guard permits shift counts up to 32, after which `mask << shift` on unsigned int is undefined behavior (shift count >= width), and the adopted sample/quantum-bits values can be bogus; this is a logic/UB flaw (CWE-682) driven directly by attacker-controlled masks.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled #define width/height values (parsed via %d and cast to guint without upper-bound checks) drive integer overflow in bytes_per_line=(ww+7)/8+padding and size=bytes_per_line*hh. This yields undersized or negative g_malloc sizes (huge allocation/abort DoS) and, in the version10p path, a 1-byte heap out-of-bounds write (e.g. size wraps to an odd value, writes size+1 bytes). evidence.reason: Integer overflow: (ww+7) wraps in unsigned arithmetic and bytes_per_line*hh wraps in signed int, producing negative or spuriously small positive sizes (CWE-190) passed to g_malloc (CWE-131/CWE-789).

evidence.snippet: for (bytes = 0, ptr = bits; bytes < size; (bytes += 2)) { if ((value = next_int (fstream)) < 0) RETURN (FALSE); *(ptr++) = value; if (!padding || ((bytes+2) % bytes_per_line)) *(ptr++) = value >> 8; }
evidence.reason: When padding==0 the loop writes 2 bytes per 2-byte step; if size wrapped to an odd value, 2*ceil(size/2)=size+1 bytes are written into a size-byte g_malloc buffer -> 1-byte heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-122/CWE-787).

evidence.snippet: *data = bits; *width = ww; *height = hh;
evidence.reason: Returns width/height that can describe billions of bytes while the allocated buffer (corrupted size) is far smaller, leaving callers to index out of bounds based on the returned dimensions.

assumptions: guint is a 32-bit unsigned int and int is 32-bit two's complement (typical GLib-based build).
MAX_SIZE is large enough that the strlen(line)==MAX_SIZE-1 guard keeps all %s sscanf tokens within name_and_type.
next_int() is a bounded reader that returns non-negative values for valid hex data and -1 on end-of-data/error.

limitations: next_int() and init_hex_table() are not shown, so only their documented contracts were assumed.
Impact beyond this function (callers indexing by returned width/height) is inferred from the returned sizes and not analyzed from caller code.

verdict.summary: Potential heap use-after-free: the remainder string node `srem` is constructed from the pointer range `[p, end)` inside the original STR_NODE buffer; the ending sequence then swaps that buffer into `top_root` and frees it via `onig_node_free(top_root)`, leaving the newly installed tree (containing `srem`) with dangling string pointers that are dereferenced later during compilation (matches Oniguruma CVE-2020-26159 pattern). Secondary: `enclen(reg->enc, p)` is applied without checking `p + len <= end`, so `onig_node_str_cat(snode, p, p + len)` can read past the buffer end for a multibyte encoding with a trailing lead byte (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: The remainder node `srem` is created from bytes that reside inside the original string node's heap buffer (`sn->s`). After `srem` is attached to the expansion tree, `swap_node(node, top_root)` moves the original STR_NODE into `top_root` and `onig_node_free(top_root)` frees that buffer. If the helper aliases the source range instead of deep-copying (Oniguruma <= 6.9.5), every `s`/`end` pointer kept in the live tree is a dangling reference -> use-after-free (CVE-2020-26159).

No bounds check verifies `p + len <= end` before reading `len` bytes. For multibyte encodings whose `enclen` returns a nominal width based on a lead byte (e.g., a trailing lead byte at the end of the buffer), `onig_node_str_cat(snode, p, p + len)` reads past `end`, and `p += len` skips the loop-termination check. Reachability depends on upstream parser validation (CWE-125).

assumptions: Standard Oniguruma semantics for `onig_node_list_add`, `onig_node_new_str`, `onig_node_str_cat`, `swap_node`, `onig_node_free`, `NODE_CAR`, and the fixed-size `items[]` array (`ONIGENC_GET_CASE_FOLD_CODES_MAX_NUM`).

The primary UAF requires `expand_case_fold_make_rem_string`/`onig_node_str_cat` to reference (borrow) the source buffer rather than deep-copy it, as in the vulnerable Oniguruma versions addressed by CVE-2020-26159.

limitations: The helper functions (`expand_case_fold_make_rem_string`, `expand_case_fold_string_alt`, `expand_case_fold_make_string`) are not shown, so their allocation/copy behavior is inferred.
No original file path/line numbers were available; the line numbers are relative to the pasted function.

verdict.summary: The trailer pointer is declared with the undefined type 'struct skb_buff' (the kernel type is 'struct sk_buff'), so the ESP output module fails to compile, and every use of 'trailer' would operate through an incompatible pointer if the symbol ever resolved. Remaining bounds depend on caller-provided tailen/tfclen/plen invariants that are not validated here.

The tailroom path returns 1 for a single linear trailer, so the returned count is inconsistent with the actual fragment layout; any downstream consumer that derives buffer sizes from this count gets an over-estimate (safe direction), but the accounting is incorrect and fragile if the expected semantics were exact.

The XBM data loops themselves appear bounds-safe: bytes_per_line is always even in the version10p path, so the 16-bit write loop cannot exceed the allocation.

match_length is built from attacker-controlled arithmetic-coded symbols and extra bits, reaching up to ~32771 (length_base max 0x3fff, length_extra max 14 bits), which can exceed the remaining space before the window end and drive the unbounded copy destination.

assumptions: window points to a heap buffer of exactly qtm->window_size bytes (no slack large enough to absorb max match_length).
window_size is 0x10000 (65536) and QTM_FRAME_SIZE allows window_posn to approach window_size before the end-of-frame/wrap handling.

Additionally, size==1 event types pass a 2-byte check but advance 4 bytes, desynchronizing the remaining-data accounting and enabling underflow in wrapped-size configurations. Exploitability depends on big-request support/max request size, but the arithmetic is unsafe on its face.

The check admits 2 bytes for size==1 events but the else branch resets size=2 and advances 4 bytes; combined with the overflowed/underflowed dataLeft this lets swaps/swapl operate beyond the request buffer, and even without overflow it mis-parses valid requests (CWE-135/CWE-697).

verdict.summary: change_indent() dereferences and advances into the current line (ptr + new_cursor_col / lbr_chartabsize) inside the insert-mode cursor-repositioning loop without any bound check against the line length or its NUL terminator, and later writes new_line[curwin->w_cursor.col] = NUL at an unvalidated column index. verdict.summary: ReadOneMNGImage trusts attacker-controlled MNG object ids. In DEFI, a 16-bit object_id is clamped with '>' so object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS (or any value clamped to it) indexes MngInfo arrays one past their end, causing a heap out-of-bounds write via exists[], frozen[], invisible[], x_off[], y_off[], and object_clip[]. The CLIP handler indexes exists[]/frozen[]/object_clip[] with an unvalidated 16-bit range, yielding out-of-bounds reads and conditional out-of-bounds writes. Additional issues: TERM/BASI/FRAM read uninitialized bytes for short chunks, several chunk handlers leak heap memory (CLON/PAST/SHOW/sBIT/pHYs/pHYg/MAGN), and MNG_LOOSE PLTE can NULL-dereference.

evidence.reason: The clamp uses '>' instead of '>='. With MNG_MAX_OBJECTS arrays (indices 0..MNG_MAX_OBJECTS-1), object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS passes the clamp and every mng_info->*[object_id] access is a heap overflow (CWE-787).

CLIP iterates first_object..last_object (up to 65535) with no MNG_MAX_OBJECTS bounds check, reading exists[]/frozen[] out of bounds and conditionally writing object_clip[i] out of bounds (CWE-125/CWE-787).
Contrast: MOVE performs the bounds check that DEFI and CLIP lack, confirming the missing validation is a defect.

TERM reads p[2] and p[6] without requiring length >= 10; short chunks cause reads of uninitialized bytes inside the length+MagickPathExtent buffer, feeding attacker-influenced garbage into delay/iteration state (CWE-457/CWE-908).

FRAM's name scan tests *p before the bound check and later mng_get_long/mng_read_box reads advance past logical length after p+=4; reads stay inside the overallocated buffer but consume uninitialized bytes (CWE-908).
These chunk handlers never RelinquishMagickMemory(chunk), leaking heap per occurrence; a crafted stream with many such chunks enables memory-exhaustion denial of service (CWE-401).
Under MNG_LOOSE, if the first branch is not taken (length==0 or length>=769) global_plte can remain NULL while the fill loop still dereferences it, causing a NULL-pointer crash (CWE-476).

assumptions: MNG_MAX_OBJECTS is 256 and the MngInfo arrays (exists, frozen, invisible, x_off, y_off, object_clip, etc.) are sized MNG_MAX_OBJECTS, making index MNG_MAX_OBJECTS out of bounds.

The branch condition and the distinct arithmetic paths (plain shift vs add-then-shift) depend on secret primes p,q and attacker-controlled x. Timing/EM observation yields Jacobi(x,p) and Jacobi(x,q) oracles, which enable factorization of n and private-key recovery.

verdict.summary: In mobi_decode_infl, the delete branch decrements pos when dir=='<' without a lower-bound check. If pos==0, pos becomes -1; the guard 'l < 0 || d + l > decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX' degenerates to a size-only check (d + l == decoded + *decoded_size), so it passes. This yields an out-of-bounds read of decoded[-1] via 'decoded[pos] != c' and an out-of-bounds write one byte before the buffer via memmove, both reachable with a minimal crafted rule stream (e.g., empty buffer followed by bytes 3 and a literal).

evidence.reason: pos underflows to -1 when pos==0 and dir=='<'. The bounds check cannot catch it because with pos=-1, l = size+1 >= 0 and d+l = decoded+size, so the comparison reduces to a check on *decoded_size alone. decoded[-1] is read before the mismatch test and memmove writes one byte at decoded-1.

evidence.snippet:
const int l = *decoded_size - pos;
if (l < 0 || d + l > decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX) { return MOBI_DATA_CORRUPT; }
evidence.reason: The guard only bounds the region end (decoded + *decoded_size) and requires l >= 0; it never validates that the starting offset d (decoded + pos) is inside the buffer, so a negative pos created by the delete-branch decrement is accepted.

assumptions: decoded points to a writable buffer and *decoded_size holds the number of valid bytes (0 <= *decoded_size <= INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX) on entry.
INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX bounds the valid buffer region; the delete underflow is out of bounds regardless of whether the bound is inclusive or exclusive.
Rule bytes are considered attacker-controlled input (e.g., from an untrusted MOBI/ebook file).
limitations: Only the provided function fragment was analyzed; no file path, line numbers, INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX definition, or call sites were shown.
End-to-end exploitability depends on how callers size/validate the decoded and rule buffers before invoking this function.
Secondary issue: debug_print with %s on a non-NUL-terminated decoded buffer may be an additional information-disclosure/crash concern, but it is not required for the main finding.

verdict.summary: r_bin_ne_get_entrypoints performs out-of-bounds heap reads while parsing the NE entry table: bundle_type is read one byte past the only checked position, segnum is read with no bound check after off is advanced, and the moveable branch reads 2 bytes via r_read_le16 after an off-by-one check (off > EntryTableLength instead of off + 1 >= EntryTableLength), allowing 1-2 byte heap over-reads on malformed NE files. Bound checks inconsistently mix r_buf_size and EntryTableLength domains. Mid-loop breaks in the moveable/fixed branches also leak the allocated RBinAddr entry on failure paths.

evidence.reason: The bounds check covers only byte `off`; the `bundle_type` read at `off+1` is unguarded, so when `tableat + off == r_buf_size(buf) - 1` a 1-byte out-of-bounds read occurs. Checks validate against `r_buf_size` while reads index `bin->entry_table`, mixing two different size domains.

The `segnum` read has no bound check at all, and the `r_read_le16` read is guarded by `off > EntryTableLength` (off-by-one): when `off == EntryTableLength` or `EntryTableLength - 1`, it reads 1-2 bytes beyond the entry table. This is a heap-based out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The subsequent `segnum > 0 && segnum < SegCount` check correctly bounds `segment_entries[segnum - 1]`.

On these `break` paths the `RBinAddr *entry` allocated at line 45 is not freed (unlike the skip branch which calls `free(entry)`), leaking heap memory for each malformed bundle that hits these bounds failures (CWE-401).

assumptions: bin->ne_header and bin->segment_entries are non-NULL and segment_entries has at least SegCount entries when the function runs; only entry_table and segments are validated here.
bin->entry_table points into or aliases the region covered by bin->buf starting at tableat; the code's mixed r_buf_size/EntryTableLength checks are the root of the mismatch.
ut64 casts on segment offset/alignment multiplication prevent overflow in paddr computation.
limitations: Exact allocation size of bin->entry_table and types of header_offset/alignment are not visible in this snippet, so the precise over-read extent depends on those definitions.
No in-bounds writes or exploitable integer overflows were identified; impact is limited to OOB reads (info disclosure/DoS) and memory leaks.
Whether bin->ne_header or bin->segment_entries can actually be NULL/undersized cannot be determined from this function alone.

verdict.summary: ljpeg_start parses attacker-controlled JPEG-like headers with unchecked fread() return values, an unsigned len underflow ((len-2) when on-disk length < 2), and no length validation before indexing data[] for SOF/SOS fields. In the 0xffc4 branch, make_decoder_ref(&dp) can advance dp past data+len and beyond the 65536-byte stack buffer, enabling an out-of-bounds read; short/truncated segments cause stale or uninitialized stack bytes to be treated as valid header fields, affecting dimensions, component counts, Huffman table state, and the final calloc.

evidence.reason: fread return values are ignored and len is a 16-bit subtraction: a segment length of 0 or 1 underflows len to 65534/65535, and a short read leaves stale or uninitialized stack bytes treated as segment payload.
data[0..7] are read without verifying len >= 8/6, so truncated segments yield stale or uninitialized values for bits, dimensions, and component count that drive later state and allocation.

evidence.reason: The bounds guard is checked only once per table; make_decoder_ref(&dp) advances dp past the data it consumes without per-byte validation, and with len near 65535 (or a short fread) dp can be advanced past data+len and beyond the end of the stack array data[0x10000], causing an out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: data[0] (SOS component count) is not validated against the actual segment length; the computed indices can read past the populated bytes, using stale or uninitialized stack data in control/state computation.

assumptions: make_decoder_ref is the typical Huffman-table builder that advances the passed pointer past the bytes it reads; its exact consumption is not shown in the provided code, so the confirmed primitive is the unchecked pointer advance past data+len.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read: the first loop iterates data[i] with step 2 and reads data[i+1] before the datalen % 2 parity check is performed. With an odd datalen, the final iteration reads one byte past the end of the client-provided cipher suite buffer when the trailing byte matches 0x00 (safe renegotiation) or 0x56 (fallback SCSV). This is a one-byte heap/stack over-read, attacker-reachable from the ClientHello, and can leak memory or crash the handshake.

evidence.reason: Loop reads data[i+1] while iterating by 2 up to datalen; when datalen is odd this reads one byte past the buffer. The even-length validation is performed later in the function, so it does not protect this loop.

The parity check executes too late: after the first loop and after server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites, both of which may perform pairwise reads on odd-length data. The check only protects the later selection loops.

assumptions: data points to exactly datalen in-bounds bytes (no implicit padding redundancy is assumed).
The trailing byte of an odd-length buffer is attacker-controlled, making the short-circuited over-read reachable.
cipher_suites_size returned by _gnutls_supported_ciphersuites is assumed even, so the local array accesses are safe.
limitations: The body of server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites is not provided; it may contain its own pairwise access on odd datalen, which would widen the over-read.
The allocation/adjacent-memory layout of data is unknown, so actual exploitability (info leak vs. crash) cannot be fully assessed from this snippet.

verdict.summary: In ReadMATImage, attacker-controlled 32-bit SizeX is multiplied by 2/4/8 in unsigned 32-bit arithmetic when computing ldblk; the wrapped value is used to allocate BImgBuff, while ImportQuantumPixels then consumes depth/8 * SizeX bytes from it, causing a heap out-of-bounds read. Additional issues: unbounded Frames loop and multi-GB allocations (resource exhaustion), undefined shift in 'one << image->depth' for 64-bit depth, and filepos advancement based on a wrapping ObjectSize+8.

evidence.reason: MATLAB_HDR.SizeX is a 32-bit unsigned file-controlled value; the multiplication occurs in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic and wraps (CWE-190) for SizeX >= 2^31 (2x), 2^30 (4x), or 2^29 (8x), yielding a small/zero ldblk that is later used for buffer sizing.

BImgBuff is sized from the wrapped ldblk, but ImportQuantumPixels reads image->columns (= unwrapped SizeX) pixels of image->depth bits from it; when ldblk wrapped, the source buffer is far too small, causing a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), e.g. 64-bit depth with SizeX=2^29 reads ~4 GiB from a ~0-byte buffer.

one=1;
image->colors = one << image->depth;
evidence.reason: For 64-bit cell types image->depth is 64; '1ULL << 64' is undefined behavior (shift count >= width), leaving the colors value unvalidated (CWE-190/CWE-682).

Frames is read from the file without any upper bound and drives the NEXT_FRAME loop, each iteration allocating new images and re-parsing file-controlled CellType, enabling resource-exhaustion denial of service (CWE-400).

evidence.snippet: filepos += MATLAB_HDR.ObjectSize + 4 + 4;
evidence.reason: ObjectSize is a 32-bit unsigned file value; 'ObjectSize + 4 + 4' is computed in 32-bit arithmetic and can wrap, causing the object parser loop to resume at an attacker-controlled wrong offset and feed unvalidated sizes into downstream processing.

assumptions: MATLAB_HDR fields such as SizeX/SizeY/ObjectSize are 32-bit unsigned integers read directly from the file with no bounds validation.
BImgBuff is used as the source buffer for ImportQuantumPixels without a per-pixel size check against the allocation.
Line numbers are approximate, derived from the provided code fragment.

The compressed-object path (DecompressBlock) and RotateImage/list-management internals were not fully expanded; they are noted only where directly relevant.

evidence.reason: getaddrinfo returns any non-zero value on failure; with positive EAI codes (macOS/BSD) the error is ignored and uninitialized servinfo is dereferenced in the loop (CWE-457, CWE-252).
errno may be clobbered by freeaddrinfo() before strerror(errno) is read, yielding stale/misleading failure diagnostics.

verdict.summary: check_passwd passes an unvalidated, attacker-controlled password length directly into the PBKDF2/HMAC-SHA1 and digest routines, uses signed-int arithmetic for the buffer allocation, and leaves the mismatch result dependent on the stored-password reader's return value, allowing memory corruption and, if any reader returns positive, fail-open authentication.

evidence.snippet:
ret = pkcs5_pbkdf2_hmac_sha1(passwd, length, salt,
			PBKDF2_SALT_LEN, PBKDF2_COUNT, keylen, passwd1_sum);
evidence.reason: length is not validated against any upper bound before being passed into pkcs5_pbkdf2_hmac_sha1, which consumes the full attacker-controlled length in the HMAC-SHA1 computation; an overlong password can overflow fixed-size internal buffers in the crypto implementation (out-of-bounds read/write, CWE-787).

evidence.snippet: passwd1_sum = calloc(hash_len * 2, sizeof(unsigned char));
evidence.reason: hash_len is int, so hash_len * 2 is computed in signed int arithmetic before conversion to size_t; a large digest_length or PBKDF2_LENGTH can overflow the multiplication and yield an undersized allocation that later digest/PBKDF2 output writes overrun (CWE-190 leading to heap overflow).

evidence.snippet:
if (!crypto_memneq(passwd1_sum, key, keylen))
			ret = 1;
evidence.reason: On a password mismatch ret is never reset to 0; it retains the value returned by read_env_passwd/read_default_passwd. If any reader returns a positive value (e.g., bytes decoded) on success, an incorrect password also yields non-zero ret, so an equality/truthiness-based caller would treat the check as passed (authentication bypass, CWE-287).

assumptions: passwd and length originate from attacker-controlled console input, with actual buffer size defined by the caller.
read_env_passwd/read_default_passwd treat their hash_len parameter as the maximum number of bytes to write.
The caller interprets a non-zero return from check_passwd as successful authentication.
limitations: Implementations of read_env_passwd, read_default_passwd, pkcs5_pbkdf2_hmac_sha1, digest_digest, and crypto_memneq are not shown, so exact bounds, return semantics, and constant-time behavior cannot be confirmed.
Config constants PBKDF2_LENGTH and PBKDF2_SALT_LEN are unknown; if PBKDF2_SALT_LEN > PBKDF2_LENGTH, keylen becomes negative and is widened to a huge size_t in the crypto call.
No explicit loops appear in this snippet; PBKDF2 iteration happens inside the external crypto routine.
The stale-ret fail-open behavior only applies if a reader can return a positive value; under a 0-on-success convention the mismatch path fails closed.

verdict.summary: Unchecked index arithmetic and missing validation can cause out-of-bounds reads/writes. Segment ids are range-checked, but num_segments is never validated as positive/bounded, output_index and input offset are not bounds-checked after computation, and the inner loop indexes flat_segment_id(i) using relative_offset_set.size() as the bound without verifying the two collections have equal cardinality. Integer overflow in flat_segment_id(i) * big_stride (CWE-190) can produce negative or oversized indices leading to heap OOB read/write (CWE-125/CWE-787).

evidence.reason: Validates each segment id against num_segments but does not validate num_segments itself (positive, sane upper bound) and does not protect the later multiplication that derives output indices.

No bounds check on output_index or offset after arithmetic. Inner loop bound is relative_offset_set.size() while flat_segment_id(i) is indexed by the same i; a cardinality mismatch (unverified helper output) causes OOB read of segment ids and OOB write into output_flat. Integer overflow in flat_segment_id(i) * big_stride can also yield negative/oversized indices.

num_segments is attacker-controllable input and is only checked for non-empty, never for positivity or magnitude, before being used to compute the output shape and as the upper bound for segment-id validation.

Derived strides/offsets are never validated against flat_segment_id.size(), flat_input.size(), or output_flat.size(); consistency is assumed but not enforced, so later indexing can exceed tensor bounds.

assumptions: INDICES_TYPE and NUM_SEGMENTS_TYPE are signed integer types (e.g., int32/int64) so the comparisons behave as shown.
GetOutputShape, GetStrides, and GetFlattenedRelativeOffsets are assumed to follow TensorFlow's UnsortedSegmentJoin semantics, but their bodies are not provided.

evidence.reason: The second instrument loop is also bounded only by unclamped insnum; s can exceed the fixed module->smp capacity, causing out-of-bounds sample access (CWE-787).

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in _gnutls_server_select_suite: the first loop iterates over the client cipher-suite list in 2-byte steps and reads data[i+1] before the datalen % 2 parity check is performed, so an odd-length list causes a read one byte past the end of the valid buffer. The parity check is sequenced after the accesses it is meant to guard.

evidence.reason: For odd datalen the final iteration (i = datalen - 1) reads data[i + 1] == data[datalen], one byte past the end of the client cipher-suite list, because no parity (or bounds) check precedes this loop. The read is unconditional in the comparison expressions.

This odd-length validation is sequenced after the first loop (lines 13-39) and after server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites() (lines 42-44), both of which already treat data as 2-byte pairs. It therefore fails to prevent the earlier out-of-bounds read and only protects the later selection loops.

assumptions: The caller provides a `data` buffer of at least `datalen` bytes (normal handshake receive path), so the direct cause of the overflow is the last-byte OOB index in the first loop for odd `datalen`, not an arbitrary wild pointer.
Helper functions such as server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites are assumed to iterate the same byte-pair structure; their exact bounds handling is not shown in the provided code.
limitations: Reachability of the unsigned loop-increment wraparound (i += 2 overflowing near UINT_MAX) depends on an unbounded datalen being passed by the caller; with message-size-bounded lengths it is not practically reachable and is not the primary issue.
Impact (information disclosure vs. crash-only DoS) depends on the surrounding heap/stack buffer layout, which is not visible in this excerpt, so severity is estimated as medium.

verdict.summary: On the ctx-allocation failure path, out_kfree_buf calls kfree() on memory allocated with vzalloc(), a mismatched memory-management routine (CWE-762). kfree() interprets the vzalloc pointer as a slab object, dereferencing invalid allocator metadata and risking kernel memory corruption or a crash when this OOM path is taken.

evidence.snippet: e->encoder_buf = vzalloc(VIDTV_S302M_BUF_SZ);
evidence.reason: The encoder buffer is allocated from the vmalloc allocator, which requires vfree() for release.

verdict.summary: No exploitable memory-safety, lifetime, or integer-safety flaw is demonstrated in the shown control flow for a valid NUL-terminated, non-aliased input. The inner loop is bounded by the NUL terminator and pointer advances are consistent. evidence.reason: The run-detection loop checks *s != NUL before decoding and advances s by clen (>=1), so s cannot pass the terminator; the shorten branch sets p = s - 1, which the outer ++p restores to s, keeping all accesses in bounds. The only flaw is that the else branch advances p by one byte while consuming clen bytes, causing continuation bytes of multi-byte characters to be re-processed; this is an output-correctness issue, not memory unsafety.

assumptions: str is a valid NUL-terminated buffer and is not aliased to gap->ga_data.
mb_cptr2char_adv/mb_ptr2char and ga_concat/ga_concat_esc are the memory-safe Vim primitives they are assumed to be.
Input strings are far below INT_MAX bytes in length.
limitations: Callers are not shown, so an aliasing precondition (str pointing into gap->ga_data) cannot be ruled out; if such a caller exists, reallocation inside ga_concat would leave p/s dangling.
Multi-byte characters are re-processed byte-by-byte in the else path after the full character is emitted, which corrupts output for multi-byte encodings.
same_len counts in int; a run longer than INT_MAX characters could overflow, but this is not realistic for the intended input sizes.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled group code 90 sets maxVertices, and the allocation size 4*maxVertices is computed in 32-bit int arithmetic without overflow checks. Also, delete[] leaves vertices dangling if the following new[] throws (use-after-free).

verdict.summary: openssl_decrypt computes the output buffer size as data_len + EVP_CIPHER_block_size() without overflow checks, allowing an attacker-controlled large input length to wrap the signed int and produce an undersized heap buffer into which EVP_DecryptUpdate/EVP_DecryptFinal write (heap OOB write). The base64 decode result is used without a NULL/negative-length check, and EVP_DecryptUpdate/set_key_length return values are ignored, with i and base64_str_len potentially uninitialized, enabling NULL dereference, out-of-bounds reads/writes, and undefined behavior.

evidence.snippet:
outlen = data_len + EVP_CIPHER_block_size(cipher_type);
outbuf = emalloc(outlen + 1);
evidence.reason: data_len is a signed int controlled by input length and can be near INT_MAX; the addition (and outlen + 1) can overflow, yielding a small/negative allocation size, then EVP_DecryptUpdate writes up to data_len bytes into outbuf, causing a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-190 -> CWE-787).

The decode result and decoded length are consumed without checking for NULL or a negative value; on decode failure data becomes NULL with a possibly -1/uninitialized data_len, which later flows into buffer sizing and EVP_DecryptUpdate, enabling NULL-pointer dereference or out-of-bounds access (CWE-476/CWE-787).

Return value of EVP_CIPHER_CTX_set_key_length is ignored; for ciphers that reject the requested key length the call fails silently and decryption proceeds with the default (possibly truncated) key while the API implies the full password is used (CWE-252, cryptographic misuse).

EVP_DecryptUpdate's success is not checked and i/outlen are assumed valid; on failure i may be uninitialized or stale, so outlen and the DecryptFinal write pointer outbuf + i can be wrong, potentially writing out of bounds (CWE-457/CWE-252).

assumptions: Line numbers are approximate; the snippet was provided without a file or line offsets.
php_openssl_validate_iv is treated as mitigating the uninitialized/NULL IV issue, but its body is out of scope.
Base64-decoding failure behavior (NULL return and/or unset ret_length) is version-dependent; the missing validation is the vulnerability regardless of exact failure semantics.
limitations: The integer overflow requires very large inputs (near INT_MAX), so exploitability depends on memory limits and whether PHP aborts on huge emalloc sizes.
No build/test environment was available to reproduce; analysis is static and based on the shown control flow.
This is PHP 5.x-era code (TSRMLS_CC, EVP_CIPHER_CTX_cleanup); modern OpenSSL/PHP versions may alter behavior.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled inode metadata flows into signed/unsigned arithmetic without range checks: `size = (*i)->data + bytes - 3` can underflow/truncate, and the outer loop combined with per-entry malloc/strdup allows unbounded heap growth and memory exhaustion during parsing of a crafted squashfs image; strdup failure is not NULL-checked and inode start/offset are not validated.

evidence.reason: `(*i)->data` is unsigned and attacker-controlled, while `size`/`bytes` are signed int. verdict.summary: gem_transmit walks guest-controlled TX descriptors in an unbounded while loop. verdict.summary: glob() recurses once per path component, per brace alternative, and per matched directory without a depth limit, and sizes stack allocations (alloca) from attacker-controlled pattern substrings (pattern_len, dirlen, home_len+dirlen). Deeply nested or very long untrusted patterns can therefore exhaust the stack or memory (DoS). No memory-corruption primitive (overflow, UAF, double-free) was found in the bounded allocation/transfer paths; a debug-build abort via assert() in the GLOB_BRACE loop is also possible if its well-formedness invariant is broken.

evidence.snippet: status = glob (dirname, ((flags & (GLOB_ERR | GLOB_NOESCAPE | GLOB_ALTDIRFUNC)) | GLOB_NOSORT | GLOB_ONLYDIR), errfunc, &dirs);
evidence.reason: Unbounded recursion: each invocation strips one path component via strrchr, and the meta branch re-enters glob per component/per matched directory. Recursion depth is directly controlled by the number of '/' characters and brace alternatives in an attacker-supplied pattern, with no depth guard.

evidence.snippet: size_t pattern_len = strlen (pattern) - 1; int alloca_onealt = glob_use_alloca (alloca_used, pattern_len); if (alloca_onealt) onealt = alloca_account (pattern_len, alloca_used);
evidence.reason: Stack buffers (onealt, dirname copies, home-dir concatenation) are allocated with alloca using sizes derived from attacker-controlled pattern content; multiplied across recursive frames this enables stack exhaustion.

evidence.reason: Relies on a brace well-formedness invariant reached only via next_brace_sub; untrusted input that violates the invariant triggers abort() in debug builds or undefined behavior in release builds.

assumptions: pattern (and flags) may originate from untrusted input, e.g., user-supplied path globs
line numbers are approximate because the snippet was provided without line markers

verdict.summary: hfsplus_block_allocate can read and write pages past the end of the allocation bitmap: the full-u32 allocation loop increments offset by PAGE_CACHE_BITS and reads the next page without an 'offset >= size' break (unlike the earlier scan loop), so on a crafted or short bitmap it treats beyond-EOF pages as free space, writes 0xffffffff into them, and yields an allocation count exceeding size-start; unvalidated size/offset and the resulting free_blocks underflow enable out-of-range block allocation and page-cache OOB read/write.

evidence.reason: Missing 'if (offset >= size) break;' after offset += PAGE_CACHE_BITS in the allocation loop. Once the last valid bitmap page is exhausted the loop unconditionally reads the next page past the bitmap end; a usable (zero-filled) page is scanned as free space, written with 0xffffffff, dirtied, and possibly followed by more pages, causing out-of-bounds read/write in the page cache and allocation results beyond size.

No validation that offset < size or that size is consistent with the actual allocation-file length before reading the first bitmap page. An attacker-controlled size/offset can select a page past the bitmap extent; the error path only catches failed reads, not valid-looking beyond-EOF pages.

Because prior loops can consume pages beyond size, *max can exceed size - start; subtracting it from free_blocks can underflow the counter, and callers then use block numbers >= size, causing out-of-range I/O and allocation-state corruption.

assumptions: PAGE_CACHE_BITS is the page size in bits (PAGE_SIZE * 8), matching the historical Linux hfsplus bitmap.c context.
size and offset are derived from on-disk HFS+ structures and are therefore attacker-influenced on a crafted image.
read_mapping_page on a block-backed file may return a usable zero-filled page for indices past end-of-file, which the code then mutates.
limitations: Callers of hfsplus_block_allocate are not shown; exploitability depends on how size/offset/len are derived and on mount privileges.
Line numbers are approximate; no exact build was available to verify against the real kernel source.
Behavior for a fully page-aligned size versus a partial last page differs, but both paths are unsafe without the missing bounds check.

verdict.summary: Heap-buffer-overflow in block_insert(): when the multibyte head-offset adjustment or the short-line append computation makes 'spaces' negative, only 'spaces' is clamped to 0 while 'count' retains a negative value. The allocation size is computed in unsigned size_t arithmetic (STRLEN + spaces + s_len + (ts_val - spaces) + count + 1), so a negative 'count' wraps and under-allocates the buffer by |count| bytes; the subsequent vim_memset/STRMOVE then writes past the end of the heap allocation.

evidence.reason: Allocation size mixes signed ints (spaces, count, ts_val) with size_t (STRLEN); a negative count wraps in unsigned arithmetic and makes the allocation smaller than the copy that follows.

evidence.snippet: if (has_mbyte && spaces > 0) { ... off = (*mb_head_off)(oldp, oldp + offset + spaces); spaces -= off; count -= off; ... } if (spaces < 0) spaces = 0;
evidence.reason: In the b_insert multibyte path, both spaces and count are decremented by off, but only spaces is clamped afterwards; count can remain negative and is later used in the allocation size.
count is assigned before the negative clamp; if end_vcol exceeds oap->end_vcol (acknowledged as possible when the cursor moved), count stays negative while spaces is clamped to 0.

evidence.snippet: mch_memmove(newp, oldp, (size_t)offset); ... vim_memset(newp + offset, ' ', (size_t)spaces); ... mch_memmove(newp + startcol, s, (size_t)s_len); ... STRMOVE(newp + offset, oldp);
evidence.reason: The copy sequence writes offset + spaces + s_len + remainder + NUL bytes based on unvalidated offsets; with the undersized allocation from a negative count this results in an out-of-bounds heap write.

assumptions: STRLEN(oldp) is strlen()/size_t, so the allocation expression is evaluated in unsigned arithmetic.
alloc() returns NULL on failure and the sizeof_needed arithmetic is not otherwise checked before copying.
block_prep(), ml_get(), mb_head_off(), and has_mbyte behave per Vim semantics; block_prep is assumed to fill bdp/oap fields, but their values are not validated in this function.
Line numbers are approximate, derived from the pasted code.
limitations: Reachability of the negative-count path depends on multibyte input contents (mb_head_off results) and on cursor/block geometry causing negative end_vcol differences; not verified by executing the code.

For valid UTF-8 the mb_head_off offset is typically bounded by char length, limiting the overflow to a few bytes; a larger overflow requires the short-line append path with a strongly negative spaces-count.

verdict.summary: When MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK is set, mdl_ticket is taken from table_list->mdl_request.ticket without a NULL check. verdict.summary: In LOCK TABLES/prelocked mode, open_table() returns success for a table whose held lock level is lower than the requested lock (best_distance < 0) without verifying that the lock satisfies the request, because the best_table path jumps to reset and returns FALSE without an error. Downstream code that trusts the positive return can operate on a table with insufficient locking, potentially bypassing LOCK TABLES read/write restrictions.

No ER_TABLE_NOT_LOCKED_FOR_WRITE or equivalent check exists in this branch, and goto reset leads to DBUG_RETURN(FALSE), i.e., successful open with an insufficient lock, enabling a LOCK TABLES restriction bypass if downstream trusts the return value.

thd->clear_error() unconditionally discards whatever error was pending when share acquisition failed, replacing it with ER_WRONG_MRG_TABLE/ER_VIEW_INVALID based only on membership flags. Genuine storage-engine or version errors (or stale unrelated errors) are masked, which can hide the real failure and mislead error handling.

The new TABLE is linked into thd->open_tables and exposed via table_list->table before vcol_fix_expr() is validated. On failure the code jumps to err_lock without unlinking the table or resetting table_list->table, leaving a partially initialized table reachable for later cleanup/processing (use-after-free or inconsistent state risk).

assumptions: Privilege checks (e.g., check_table_access) are performed by callers and are out of scope for this snippet.
thd->locked_tables_mode values (LTM_LOCK_TABLES/LTM_PRELOCKED) follow standard MySQL semantics.

verdict.summary: In the USB_DT_OTG descriptor branch of composite_setup(), config is picked via list_first_entry(&cdev->configs, ...) when cdev->config is NULL; the following 'if (!config) goto done;' is dead code because list_first_entry() never returns NULL. If the configs list is empty (or the first config's descriptor array is shorter than 18/25 bytes), reading config->descriptors[0] and copying otg_desc_len bytes into req->buf dereferences an invalid pointer, enabling a host-triggered kernel crash or limited kernel memory disclosure.

evidence.reason: list_first_entry() returns a non-NULL bogus pointer on an empty list, so the 'if (!config)' guard never fires; config->descriptors[0] is then dereferenced with no validation and up to 25 bytes are copied from invalid/unrelated memory into req->buf, giving an out-of-bounds read/invalid dereference reachable via a host USB GET_DESCRIPTOR(OTG) control request.

assumptions: Reaching the flawed path requires gadget_is_otg(gadget) to be true and cdev->config to be NULL, i.e., a GET_DESCRIPTOR(OTG) request sent while the device is unconfigured.
The invalid dereference only manifests when cdev->configs is empty or when the first config's descriptors[0] allocation is shorter than the copied otg_desc_len (18/25 bytes).
Helper routines (config_desc, get_string, bos_desc, fill_ext_compat, fill_ext_prop) are assumed to bound their writes to the request buffer; they are not present in the provided code.
limitations: The dead 'if (!config) goto done;' guard shows the intent was to handle the empty case, but it is ineffective by construction; reachability in practice depends on whether a composite device can be bound with zero configurations.
Impact is an invalid read (crash / possible info leak) rather than a write overflow; standard descriptor, interface, status, and OS-descriptor paths are correctly size-bounded in the shown code.
No kernel version or exact triggering environment is given, so exploitability as remote DoS vs. local-only test-harness crash cannot be fully established.

verdict.summary: sctp_sf_violation_chunklen forwards an already-invalid, attacker-controlled chunk (arg) to sctp_sf_abort_violation without revalidating its length and without a NULL-asoc guard (unlike sctp_sf_violation_chunk). The ABORT-construction path dereferences the malformed chunk and the association, enabling out-of-bounds reads on truncated packets and a NULL-pointer dereference on out-of-the-blue (asoc==NULL) paths.

evidence.snippet: static sctp_disposition_t sctp_sf_violation_chunklen(const struct sctp_endpoint *ep, const struct sctp_association *asoc, const sctp_subtype_t type, void *arg, sctp_cmd_seq_t *commands)
evidence.reason: Handler is reached after the chunk's length is already known invalid; it performs no bounds/length revalidation before passing arg (the malformed chunk) into the ABORT builder, so truncated packets can drive reads past the actual data (OOB read).

evidence.snippet: return sctp_sf_abort_violation(ep, asoc, arg, commands, err_str, sizeof(err_str));
evidence.reason: asoc is forwarded unconditionally; without an `if (!asoc)` discard guard, an out-of-the-blue chunk-length violation (asoc==NULL) leads to a NULL-pointer dereference inside sctp_sf_abort_violation/sctp_make_abort.

assumptions: sctp_sf_abort_violation dereferences both asoc and arg while constructing the ABORT (standard Linux kernel SCTP implementation via sctp_make_abort).
The SCTP state machine can dispatch this handler on out-of-the-blue packets where asoc == NULL.
limitations: Only the snippet was provided; the bodies of sctp_sf_abort_violation and the dispatcher were not available for direct verification.
The exact reachability of the asoc==NULL path and whether the abort helper bounds-checks the chunk copy depend on kernel version and surrounding code not shown here.

verdict.summary: Crafted LZW-compressed input can trigger out-of-bounds writes during decompression: the code-to-string expansion loop decrements stackp past the start of the fixed-size de_stack with no lower-bound check (chain length can reach 2^BITS), the classic gzip unlzw buffer overflow enabling memory corruption / potential code execution; additionally, posbits realignment at resetbuf can make insize negative so read_buffer writes before inbuf, and a CLEAR code does not reset oldcode, leaving stale prefixes in the dictionary logic.

evidence.reason: No bounds check limits how far stackp may descend below de_stack. A chain of up to maxmaxcode (2^BITS) codes is traversed, pushing one char per iteration; with a fixed de_stack capacity smaller than that (classic gzip), *--stackp performs an out-of-bounds write below the buffer, corrupting adjacent memory (CWE-787/CWE-121).

posbits is realigned upward to a code boundary (lines 82-83, 105-106) and can exceed the number of valid bits, so e = insize - (posbits>>3) may become negative. insize is then set negative and read_buffer writes INBUFSIZ bytes at inbuf+insize, i.e. before the start of inbuf (out-of-bounds write), with subsequent bit reads misaligned.

oldcode is not reset to -1 after a CLEAR, so the next symbol is decoded via the stale-prefix path and new table entries are built with a pre-CLEAR code (line 176); the KwKwK special case may then traverse dictionary slots that were not re-initialized, weakening the code < free_ent invariant relied on by the chain-walk loop.

assumptions: de_stack is a fixed-size buffer and its declared capacity is smaller than the maximum chain length 2^BITS (classic gzip unlzw layout); with BITS=16 the chain can reach 65536 characters.
read_buffer writes INBUFSIZ bytes at the given offset and gzip_error/read_error terminate the process.
The input() macro advances posbits by n_bits per code and bitmask bounds n_bits <= BITS via the earlier maxbits > BITS check.
limitations: Definitions of de_stack, inbuf, outbuf, OUTBUFSIZ, INBUFSIZ, MAXCODE, and the tab_* macros are not shown in the provided code, so exact overflow sizes and the inbuf underflow reachability depend on those (unseen) declarations.
The outbuf copy loop (lines 151-171) and table insertion guard (line 174) were analyzed and appear bounded.
The DEBUG-only read of p[-1] (line 126) is compiled out in release builds and not counted as a primary finding.

verdict.summary: Off-by-one out-of-bounds write in glob()'s GLOB_TILDE '~user/...' handling: the user-name buffer is allocated with (end_name - dirname) bytes, but the non-unescape copy writes (end_name - dirname) bytes (including the '/' separator) and then writes the terminating NUL one byte past the end of the allocation, corrupting adjacent heap (malloc path) or stack (alloca path) memory. The copied string also wrongly includes the '/' separator, so the subsequent getpwnam() lookup fails.

evidence.reason: newp is allocated with exactly (end_name - dirname) bytes. mempcpy writes that many bytes (the user name plus the '/' separator) and the NUL is then written at index (end_name - dirname), one byte past the end -> heap/stack out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It also yields user_name 'name/', so getpwnam() cannot resolve the intended user.
Confirms the allocated size equals end_name - dirname, which only fits the user name plus NUL; the copy of (end_name - dirname) bytes plus the NUL overruns the buffer by one byte.

assumptions: A pattern of the form '~user/...' with GLOB_TILDE or GLOB_TILDE_CHECK reaches the analyzed branch (dirname[1] is neither '\0' nor '/' nor an escaped '/').

Helper functions not shown (glob_in_dir, next_brace_sub, prefix_array, glob_use_alloca, is_dir, __glob_pattern_type, collated_compare) follow standard glibc implementations and contribute no additional overflow in this path.
A plain '~user' pattern takes the direct user_name = dirname + 1 path and is not affected by this off-by-one.
limitations: The code was provided inline, so no file path or reliable line numbers are available; evidence locations are null.

Actual impact depends on allocator layout: the heap overwrite lands in the next chunk's metadata only when the usable size equals the request size (end_name - dirname of form 16k-8); otherwise it typically lands in allocator slack. The alloca path overwrites one byte of adjacent stack storage.
Deeply nested GLOB_BRACE or long metachar dirname chains can cause deep recursion (potential stack exhaustion / DoS), but this is not conclusively demonstrated from the supplied code alone.
Other arithmetic paths (GLOB_DOOFFS, GLOB_NOCHECK, GLOB_MARK, brace scratch buffer, tilde-HOME merge) were checked and appear correctly bounded.

verdict.summary: In hfsplus_block_allocate, the allocation phase's page-crossing loop advances offset past the end of the bitmap file without an 'offset >= size' check (unlike the scan phase) and calls read_mapping_page for a page beyond EOF, then kmaps and dirties it. Combined with unchecked read_mapping_page return values, a crafted HFS+ filesystem can trigger out-of-bounds page access, a kernel crash (ERR_PTR dereference), or writeback/block-accounting corruption beyond the allocation file.

evidence.snippet: set_page_dirty(page); kunmap(page); offset += PAGE_CACHE_BITS; page = read_mapping_page(mapping, offset / PAGE_CACHE_BITS, NULL); pptr = kmap(page); curr = pptr; end = pptr + PAGE_CACHE_BITS / 32;
evidence.reason: Second (allocation) loop crosses to the next page unconditionally when curr reaches end; unlike the first loop (lines 53-56) it lacks an 'offset >= size' break, so it reads/kmaps/dirties a page past the end of the bitmap file when the run ends exactly at a page boundary.

evidence.snippet: page = read_mapping_page(mapping, offset / PAGE_CACHE_BITS, NULL); pptr = kmap(page);
evidence.reason: read_mapping_page() return value is not checked for IS_ERR before kmap(); a beyond-EOF read returns an error pointer that kmap dereferences, causing a kernel oops.

evidence.snippet: end = pptr + ((size + 31) & (PAGE_CACHE_BITS - 1)) / 32;
evidence.reason: When size is within 31 bits of the page end, (size + 31) & (PAGE_CACHE_BITS - 1) wraps to a small value (0), under-counting the words in the final page; the scan then skips the last partial page and wrongly reports the bitmap as full (incorrect allocation, DoS).

evidence.snippet: *max = offset + (curr - pptr) * 32 + i - start; HFSPLUS_SB(sb).free_blocks -= *max;
evidence.reason: After the beyond-EOF page access, *max is derived from an out-of-range page offset, and subtracting it from free_blocks can underflow the free-block counter, corrupting subsequent allocation decisions.

assumptions: PAGE_CACHE_BITS = PAGE_SIZE * 8 (32768 for 4096-byte pages), and the allocation file contains ceil(size / PAGE_CACHE_BITS) pages.
read_mapping_page() returns ERR_PTR for pages beyond EOF on block device mappings, or may return a zero page depending on kernel version and mapping.
The function operates under the alloc-file mutex, so the race surface between phases is limited to the unchecked page reads.
limitations: Code is analyzed statically without execution or a specific kernel version; exact crash vs. writeback behavior depends on page-cache and block-device mapping semantics.
The provided snippet omits definitions (PAGE_CACHE_BITS, HFSPLUS_SB, allocation-file initialization), so bounds are inferred from the standard kernel definitions.
Severity assumes a local attacker who can mount a crafted HFS+ filesystem; no privilege escalation is demonstrated.

verdict.summary: unlzw reconstructs LZW output strings on a fixed de_stack buffer using *--stackp pushes that are never bounds-checked against the start of the buffer. An attacker-controlled compressed stream can drive the prefix-chain length (plus the KwKwK extra character) beyond de_stack capacity, underflowing the buffer and corrupting adjacent memory — matching the historically exploited gzip unlzw stack-buffer overflow (CVE-2001-1228 / CVE-2002-0059).

evidence.reason: Unbounded writes: each iteration decrements stackp with no test that stackp still points inside de_stack. The loop terminates only when code < 256; the chain depth is entirely attacker-controlled (up to maxmaxcode ~ 2^16 entries). If the reconstructed chain exceeds de_stack capacity, memory before de_stack is overwritten (CWE-121/CWE-787).

The KwKwK special case pushes one extra character and then walks the full chain of oldcode. The guard (code > free_ent) validates only the code value, not the resulting chain depth or the stackp position, so this path adds one more character than a plain chain and compounds the de_stack underflow.

DEBUG-only out-of-bounds read: after posbits -= n_bits, p = &inbuf[posbits>>3] can point before inbuf when posbits < n_bits, and p[-1]..p[3] read outside the buffer (CWE-125). Non-DEBUG builds are unaffected.

Sequence flaw: the CLEAR branch jumps to resetbuf, skipping `oldcode = incode;` (line 181), so oldcode retains a pre-CLEAR code. A subsequent code == free_ent (256) triggers the KwKwK path and walks the chain of that stale code through the just-cleared table, reading logically-uninitialized tab_prefix/tab_suffix entries (garbage output). Lower severity than the de_stack overflow, and not out-of-array bounds by itself.

assumptions: de_stack is a fixed-size buffer declared outside the shown snippet (historically a stack array in gzip's unlzw), and its capacity is not verified against the maximum possible chain length.
Macro/type defaults follow gzip: BITS=16, MAXCODE(n)=(1<<n), INIT_BITS=9, FIRST=257, INBUF_EXTRA padding, OUTBUFSIZ flush size.
An attacker fully controls maxbits (0..16) and the code stream, and therefore the dictionary growth and prefix-chain lengths.
limitations: The declaration/size of de_stack, inbuf, outbuf, tab_prefix/tab_suffix and the exact macro definitions (input, MAXCODE, clear_tab_prefixof) are outside the provided snippet, so exact overflow distance cannot be computed.
The de_stack overflow is demonstrated as an unbounded write with no enforced upper bound; concrete exploitability depends on the missing buffer size.
The DEBUG-only out-of-bounds read (p[-1]..p[3]) manifests only in DEBUG builds.
The CLEAR-path stale-oldcode issue is a correctness flaw that produces undefined dictionary reads rather than proven memory corruption.

verdict.summary: ip6gre_err handles remote ICMPv6 errors without validating the attacker-influenced 'offset' and without ensuring the encap-limit TLV offset lies inside the region guaranteed linear by pskb_may_pull. In the ICMPV6_PARAMPROB branch, the offset returned by ip6_tnl_parse_tlv_enc_lim (bounded only by skb->len) is dereferenced via skb->data[teli] beyond the pulled (offset+grehlen) linear area, allowing an out-of-bounds read when the skb tail is paged/non-linear. Additionally, ICMPV6_PKT_TOOBIG computes mtu = be32_to_cpu(info) - offset in u32, which underflows to a huge value and is assigned to t->dev->mtu, letting a remote peer inflate the tunnel MTU.

evidence.reason: The TLV parse walks attacker-controlled type/length bytes from skb->data and returns teli bounded only by skb->len, while this function only pulled offset+grehlen bytes. The dereference &skb->data[teli] and read of tel->encap_limit access data beyond the guaranteed linear region (the encap-limit TLV is inside the tunneled payload past the GRE header), enabling an out-of-bounds read if the skb tail is non-linear; teli and info are both attacker-steerable (CWE-125).

mtu is unsigned 32-bit; with attacker-controlled info smaller than offset the subtraction underflows to a value near 4G. The lower-bound clamp does not catch it, so the unbounded value is written to t->dev->mtu, allowing a remote peer to inflate the tunnel MTU (CWE-190).

offset is attacker-influenced and only used in signed int arithmetic; negative or overflowing offset defeats the pull guarantees, and the fixed-size dereferences of ipv6h->saddr/daddr and greh->protocol are assumed covered without any explicit offset >= 0 or offset+grehlen <= skb->len validation (CWE-125/CWE-190).

assumptions: The snippet is the Linux kernel net/ipv6/ip6_gre.c ICMPv6 error handler for IPv6 GRE tunnels.
offset and info are directly or indirectly derived from remote ICMPv6 traffic and are treated as attacker-influenced.
ip6_tnl_parse_tlv_enc_lim bounds its TLV walk by skb->len but does not linearize the skb; data past offset+grehlen may be paged/non-linear.
A matching IPv6 GRE tunnel must exist for execution to reach the switch.
limitations: Caller-side constraints on offset (e.g., icmpv6_notify/embedded-header parsing) are outside the provided snippet and may bound offset in practice.
Reachability of the OOB read depends on the skb layout (fragmented/paged receive); on fully linear skbs the dereference stays within skb->len.
The helper function body and struct definitions (ipv6_tlv_tnl_enc_lim, gre_base_hdr) are not shown; their exact semantics are inferred.

verdict.summary: Heap buffer overflow in eval_string(): the output buffer is sized from the counted source length plus a hard-coded 5-byte reserve per '\<...>' special key, without accounting for multi-modifier/non-simplified keys or any divergence between find_special_key() (counting pass) and trans_special() (copy pass). trans_special() writes into the buffer before the only bounds check, which itself permits end == base+len before the NUL terminator is written, so crafted string literals can cause an out-of-bounds heap write; interpolated {{/}} handling can also drive 'extra' negative, shrinking the allocation.

evidence.snippet:
len = (int)(p - *arg + extra);
rettv->vval.v_string = alloc(len);
evidence.reason: Destination size is a byte-count plus a per-key expansion heuristic (extra += 5 at line 23). If a '\<...>' key expands beyond 9 bytes from 4 counted input bytes (multi-modifier or non-simplified forms), or if the counting pass under-counts the form, alloc(len) under-allocates and the copy loop writes past the heap buffer.

trans_special() writes to 'end' before any bounds verification; the check only emits an error after the overflow has occurred. The comparison 'end >= base + len' also allows end == base+len, after which '*end = NUL' (line 164) is an out-of-bounds write one byte past the allocation.

Each {{/}} pair decrements the allocation reserve; with enough escaped pairs (or few special keys), 'extra' becomes negative and len at line 63 can be smaller than the data the copy loop emits, assuming reductions are realized exactly. The correctness depends on the two passes consuming bytes identically, which is not enforced.

assumptions: find_special_key()/trans_special() follow Vim semantics: they parse '\<...>' key forms and report consumed bytes/output length as described in the comments.
FSK_KEYCODE/FSK_IN_STRING/FSK_SIMPLIFY behave as standard Vim flags affecting special-key expansion width.
mb_char2bytes()/MB_COPY_CHAR()/MB_PTR_ADV() operate on the active 'encoding', with UTF-8 multibyte sequences of at most a few bytes.
limitations: The callers of eval_string() and the exact reachable inputs are not in scope, so exploitability of the worst-case key expansion is inferred rather than demonstrated.
The real upper bounds of trans_special() output and find_special_key() consumption are not defined in the provided code, limiting precise proof of the overflow trigger.
The int truncation at line 63 is only reachable for impractical literal sizes and is noted as a secondary issue.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in block_insert(): in the append/is_short path, 'count' is set from an unvalidated 'spaces' that can be negative; the clamp at line 60 zeroes 'spaces' but leaves 'count' negative, so the allocation size (line 64) is under-sized by |count| while the actual writes (memmove of s, STRMOVE NUL) still use the full offsets, overflowing the heap buffer.

evidence.reason: 'count' is assigned the pre-clamp, possibly negative 'spaces' (line 51); after 'spaces' is clamped to 0 (line 60), 'count' is not adjusted, so the unsigned size expression at lines 64-66 includes a negative term that shrinks the heap allocation below the real requirement.

Since 'spaces' is 0 after clamping, the negative 'count' is never added to 'offset' (line 99 guard), so the writes exceed the under-sized allocation, producing an out-of-bounds heap write.

assumptions: Reachable input state requires append mode (b_insert == 0) on a line flagged is_short with (oap->end_vcol - bdp->end_vcol + 1) < 0, which the code comment itself states can happen when the cursor was moved.
All size arithmetic is evaluated in size_t width because STRLEN() yields size_t; otherwise the negative terms would not wrap to a small positive allocation in an obviously-under-allocated way.
Line numbers are relative to the provided snippet since no file path was supplied.
limitations: Exact exploitability depends on caller invariants in block_prep() and ml_get()/ml_replace() that are outside this snippet.
No execution or crash repro was performed; analysis is based on static control-flow and size accounting.
The insert-mode is_short skip (line 23) and the positive-spaces TAB-split branches were checked and do not under-allocate in the same way, so the finding is scoped to the append/is_short path.
